title: Meta launches personal AI agent, Muse, emphasizes safety and privacy
summary: Meta is launching a personal artificial intelligence agent, Muse, for people 18 and over
story: Meta is launching a personal artificial intelligence agent, Muse, for people 18 and over

Meta launched on Tuesday a personal artificial intelligence agent, Muse, for people 18 and over who are looking for help with day-to-day tasks like schedules, shopping and, in the company's words, turning “long-term goals into action plans.”

The parent company of Instagram and Facebook is stressing the safety and privacy features of the agent, which for now is only available in the U.S. Muse, Meta said, runs on a dedicated, secure virtual machine that houses both the agent and the user's data.

People can message the agent in a separate app, called Muse, or message it in WhatsApp. It can handle simple tasks like sending an email or booking travel, or bigger, long-term goals like creating a yearlong exercise plan or setting up a new business.

“Once a person shares a goal with Muse, it helps them develop a personalized plan and coordinate their time and resources, then advances the work on its own. It can open a browser, fill out forms, and negotiate on their behalf,” Meta said in a blog post.
Tech companies are touting AI agents as the next step after chatbots, which can answer questions and retrieve information but won't take action on the user's behalf.

At its most basic level, an AI agent works like a traditional, human-crafted computer program that executes a job, like launching an application. Combined with an AI large language model, however, it can search for knowledge that enables it to complete tasks without explicit, step-by-step instructions. That means, instead of just helping you draft the language of an email, it can theoretically handle the whole process — receiving a message from your coworker, figuring out what you might want to say, and firing off the response on its own.
For Meta, the agent fits into CEO Mark Zuckerberg's vision of AI superintelligence that's available to “everyone.” He outlined his vision last month in a 6,500-word essay published online.

In the document derided by critics as fantastical, Zuckerberg said his company is working toward an era where everyone will have the tools to create new businesses, receive Ph.D.-level tutoring and provide personalized lifestyle tips.

“Everyone will have an exceptionally capable personal agent that understands you, your goals, and everything you care about. Your agent will work 24/7 on your behalf to improve your relationships, health, career, finances, home management, hobbies, and more,” Zuckerberg wrote. “It will free up time for the things you enjoy, and help you accomplish more than you could otherwise.”
The question is, will people actually use it?

title: China's Huawei Technologies faces racketeering trial in New York
summary: The world's biggest supplier of telecommunications network gear faces a criminal trial in New York
story: The world's biggest supplier of telecommunications network gear faces a criminal trial in New York

NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Huawei Technologies, a leading Chinese tech company, faces a criminal racketeering trial in New York over charges that it stole technology, plotted to steal U.S. trade secrets and committed wire and bank fraud, among other crimes.
Jury selection is scheduled to begin Tuesday.

The indictment alleges that, besides stealing trade secrets, Huawei and some of its subsidiaries did business in North Korea despite U.S. sanctions there and installed surveillance equipment that helped Iran spy on protesters during 2009 anti-government demonstrations in Iran.

Huawei’s lawyers have tried to get the broad criminal case dismissed, arguing in court filings that the U.S. allegations were too vague and impermissibly tried to extend American authority abroad. The company said in a statement that the narrative pushed by U.S. prosecutors is “demonstrably false.”
“Long-term investment in innovation, backed by the utmost respect for intellectual property, has been the driving force behind Huawei’s business success,” the company said.

Huawei is the world's biggest supplier of gear for wireless telecom networks but the company is banned from selling equipment to U.S. carriers over fears it poses a security risk. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies like Canada and Britain.

The company makes phones and other consumer electronics but has been cut off from other lines of business. More recently, it has expanded into chipmaking as the boom in artificial intelligence fuels demand for microprocessors.

During President Donald Trump's first term in office, his administration raised national security concerns about Huawei and began lobbying Western allies against including the company's products in their next-generation high-speed wireless networks. The U.S. announced the criminal charges in early 2019 and has since expanded the allegations.
Chinese officials said the U.S. government has engaged in “economic bullying” and improperly used national security as a pretext for “oppressing Chinese companies.”

U.S. prosecutors accused Huawei of using a Hong Kong shell company known as Skycom to sell equipment to Iran in violation of U.S. sanctions. They also charged its chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, with fraud, saying she misled HSBC bank about the company’s business dealings in Iran.

Meng, the daughter of Huawei’s founder, was arrested in Canada in late 2018 on a U.S. extradition request but released in September 2021 in a high-stakes prisoner swap that freed two Canadians held by China and allowed her to return home.
As part of the deal, the U.S. dropped its extradition request and said it would dismiss the fraud charges against Meng.

The biggest maker of network gear, Huawei struggled to hold onto its market share under sanctions that have blocked its access to most U.S. processor chips and other technology. The limits led it to ramp up its own development of computer chips and other advanced technologies.

title: Japan protests as China slaps new measures against exports of key chipmaking material
summary: Japan has protested Chinese controls that will limit its exports of a key chemical used to make computer chips
story: Japan has protested Chinese controls that will limit its exports of a key chemical used to make computer chips

BANGKOK -- Japan has protested against Chinese controls that will limit its exports of a key chemical used to make computer chips, saying Tuesday that Tokyo is studying the potential impact on Japanese companies.
China imposed the curb on imports of dichlorosilane from Japan, saying its exports of the material, also known as DCS, have violated anti-dumping regulations and harmed China’s domestic industry.

Beginning Tuesday, companies importing the chemical compound from Japan must provide cash deposits to China’s customs at rates of up to 99.2%. The measure applies to Shin-Etsu Chemical and Denal Silane, among other Japanese exporters of DCS.
Beijing says the measure is provisional as an investigation continues. A final ruling will come later.

Relations between China and Japan have been strained since November, when Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi angered Beijing by suggesting Japan's military could intervene if China used military force on Taiwan, a self-ruled island Beijing claims as its territory.

In Tokyo, Japan’s top government spokesperson, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara, protested against the controls and said Tokyo would “respond appropriately” to avoid unfair harm to Japanese companies.

China’s commerce ministry launched its anti-dumping probe into Japanese DCS as part of various measures against Japan. Beijing has also imposed export controls on Japanese firms for dual-use items that can be used for military purposes.

DCS is used in a chemical vapor process to put thin layers of silicon, oxide, or other films in semiconductor logic and memory chips. The global market for DCS is highly competitive, but Japan is the leading producer of ultrapure DCS for computer chip fabrication.
Yamaguchi reported from Tokyo.

title: 'Divorce-tok' fills social media as creators find audiences by sharing heartbreak
summary: Many influencers are sharing their divorce journeys on social media, using platforms like TikTok and Instagram to connect with others
story: Many influencers are sharing their divorce journeys on social media, using platforms like TikTok and Instagram to connect with others
On Instagram feeds that are often teeming with curated, contrived content, a recent post from Monette Wagner stood out for her disarming openness.
Looking into the camera, Wagner, a 36-year-old mother of three, said in the video: “Divorce can feel like a death.”

In what resembles a digital journal, Wagner has posted videos in real time about the emotions and life changes that have come with her recent divorce. Developing financial independence, getting used to co-parenting, and moving on from heartbreak are frequent themes of her Instagram posts.

A growing number of people, the majority of them women, are sharing unvarnished divorce stories, both offering and seeking advice on social media. Moving beyond a stigma around discussing marital breakdowns, the content provides a space for the creators to heal, and for their followers to relate and reflect on their own experiences and emotions.
A professional photographer in Indianapolis, Wagner already had a platform on Instagram to share and promote her work. But she recently took the page in this more vulnerable direction.

Alongside posts about the heavier moments, she also shares lessons learned and more optimistic musings. She has posted about wanting to reconnect with the confident, curious person she was more than a decade ago — before she met her now-former husband. She's revisiting passions she had as a teen, including skateboarding and learning to DJ.

“I wanted to show my kids that you can still be strong even through these hard days. I wanted to show them how strong hope is,” she said. “I feel more confident. I feel resilient. I feel like I faced my fears of showing up scared, of putting myself out there as my authentic self.”
On TikTok, where niche categories of content sometimes earn a nickname, content that delves into marital woes has been dubbed “divorce-tok.”

The level of detail creators choose to divulge about their divorce and marriage varies widely. Some, like Wagner, do not post about their ex-partners. Others provide detailed accounts of issues in their marriage and the sometimes messy and lengthy process of finalizing their divorce.

The voyeuristic world of social media tends to love story-time-style videos where creators talk as if they’re chatting on the phone with a friend, sparing no details. Some creators post one-off videos, while others make it the focus on their platforms. Trends related to divorce also periodically pop up online, like this season’s “hot divorcée summer” videos and clips showing people’s post-divorce “glow-ups,” or physical, and in many cases, emotional, transformations. The #divorce hashtag has millions of posts on both TikTok and Instagram.

Jen Hamilton, a labor and delivery nurse with more than 5 million TikTok followers, recently has been sharing the “nitty-gritty” details behind her divorce, as she said in one video. Hamilton has explained how her husband led what she called a “double life” with another partner, and has shared videos of herself crying, cracking jokes and generally processing the news while maintaining her signature optimism.

In a more celebratory post, Hamilton shared photos and videos from what would have been her 14th wedding anniversary, recognizing the occasion with what she called a “Jendependence Day” party. More than a dozen friends and co-workers joined her at her North Carolina home as she burned her bedsheets and toasted to her future beyond her marriage.

“I feel like if I share my pain with you, I don’t feel so alone, because there’s so many other people going through the exact same thing,” she said in a video in July. She added that her followers then, in turn, feel less alone too.
Some men have posted content along these lines, but women make up the vast majority of creators posting about divorce.

Many of these creators say they’re not sharing their stories in hopes of gaining pity or sympathy, but rather are hoping to develop a sense of community online with people who have gone through similar experiences.

Alex Daly, a 41-year-old creator in Philadelphia, started posting about her divorce around three years after she went through it. Once she found that she had processed her emotions around the divorce, she was eager to talk about it. She aims to reach people who are “still in the thick of it, because it’s a really hard place to be,” she said.

“It can feel very lonely and isolating. It can feel like you’re the only person going through it,” Daly said. Followers have thanked her and told her she's saying what they’ve been thinking and feeling. “You’re making me feel normal,” she said some people message her.

It seems paradoxical that a topic that can be difficult or awkward to discuss with family and friends is also one some feel comfortable sharing with potentially millions of strangers online. But it can be much easier to forge digital connections than in-person ones, according to Tasha R. Dunn, an associate professor at the University of Toledo. Dunn researches the relationship between lived experiences and media, including how we present our lives on social media.

“There are few divorce support groups in a given community, but you have something at the tip of your fingers on your phone or computer where you can find people who’ve literally shared your same experience,” Dunn said.
“People maybe feel a little bit safer to put that content out there rather than to have a physical town hall and say, ’Everybody come, I’m going to share my experience.'”
The candor that makes divorce-related content so popular could also be detrimental for those posting if they’re in the midst of legal proceedings.

Jackie Combs, a matrimonial and family law attorney in Los Angeles, said she does not recommend that people share anything related to their divorce, especially personal grievances or intimate details, publicly online.
“Every single reel that you put out there, every piece of content that’s related to it, you have to presume that somebody is watching and is going to use it as evidence, if needed,” she said.

On social media, Combs herself often shares content about divorce, speaking about the importance of financial independence and prenuptial agreements. She said she sees social media as a key part of the “destigmatization” of divorce to show people it's “not the end, it’s just a pivot.”
Creators like Wagner and Daly also can be the subject of intense trolling and negativity.

Daly said she's received comments and messages from people saying she's “ruining people’s lives” or that she doesn't have morals. She said she tries not to let those comments or interactions get to her because those people don't know what happened in the privacy of her marriage or who she truly is.

The negativity is “just proving that there is still a stigma and a taboo around divorce,” Daly said. So it keeps her motivated to “share about how divorce just doesn’t have to be the end of your life and how it can actually be an amazing beginning.”

title: Indonesia keeps several airports closed though volcanic eruption is easing
summary: Indonesia is maintaining closures at several airports and shifting schools to remote learning though the eruption of Anak Krakatau is easing
story: Indonesia is maintaining closures at several airports and shifting schools to remote learning though the eruption of Anak Krakatau is easing

JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesia extended the closure of several airports and shifted schools to remote learning in affected areas on Monday even though a volcanic eruption that has halted nearly 3,000 flights and coated areas with ash was subsiding.

The continuous, 25-hour eruption of Anak Krakatau that produced a fountain of lava and a boom heard 700 kilometers (435 miles) away ended Sunday, the country's Geological Agency said. But it remained active Monday with moderate, intermittent eruptions, dark ash emissions and small, localized earthquakes.

Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said Monday that authorities decided to extend the temporary closure of seven airports until midnight from an earlier deadline of 6 p.m., despite improving conditions at some facilities. Previously, Atung Bungsu Airport in Pagar Alam, a city in South Sumatra province, resumed normal operations Monday morning.

"We are taking a conservative approach because wind direction is highly dynamic,” Purwagandhi said in a statement. “We want to ensure that volcanic ash has moved away from airports around Anak Krakatau.”
Although tests at several airports showed no traces of volcanic ash, operations will not resume until further assessments are completed, Purwagandhi said.
He said the extended closure would also allow airport operators and airlines to inspect and clean runways, taxiways, aprons and aircraft that may have been exposed to volcanic ash.
The government also authorized schools in areas affected by volcanic ash to shift temporarily to online learning to reduce students’ exposure to ash.

Anak Krakatau is a volcanic island in the Sunda Strait between Indonesia's main islands of Java and Sumatra. Its name means “child of Krakatau,” and the volcano is the offspring of the infamous Krakatau, whose monumental 1883 eruption triggered a period of global cooling.
An eruption of Anak Krakatau in 2018 caused a tsunami that killed at least 430 people in Sumatra and Java.

Indonesia has more than 120 active volcanoes and frequently experiences eruptions due to its location along the Pacific “Ring of Fire,” the ring of seismic faults around the Pacific Ocean where most global seismic activity occurs.

title: Assad-era Syrian reactor was configured for nuclear weapons, IAEA chief says
summary: The Assad-era government in Syria was constructing a nuclear reactor that was configured to produce fissile material for possible use in nuclear weapons, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency
story: The Assad-era government in Syria was constructing a nuclear reactor that was configured to produce fissile material for possible use in nuclear weapons, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency

VIENNA -- The Assad-era government in Syria was constructing a nuclear reactor that was configured to produce fissile material for possible use in nuclear weapons, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency said on Monday.

The “configuration” and the “technical features” of the nuclear reactor under construction in Syria during the leadership of ousted former President Bashar Assad were “very efficient in the production of fissile material that could be directly used for the fabrication of nuclear weapons,” IAEA director general Rafael Grossi said.

“Of course, that was never declared, that was always denied, so, and again, intentions cannot be judged, but that was a very serious proliferation concern that we had, and this has been difficult work,” he told reporters on the first day of a regular meeting of the IAEA Board of Governors, in Vienna.
Syria was believed to have operated an extensive undeclared nuclear program under Assad that included a nuclear reactor built by North Korea in eastern Deir el-Zour province.
Following Assad’s ouster, the new government agreed to give IAEA inspectors access to suspected former nuclear sites.

During a visit to Syria in August, IAEA inspectors confirmed that “the cooling infrastructure which has now been uncovered is consistent with that of a nuclear reactor.” Grossi and a team of senior inspectors also visited a previously undeclared site in the country.

Syria notified the agency of the site’s existence in a July 17 letter and invited the IAEA “to cooperate with the Syrian authorities in the inspection and verification of the site and of any nuclear material to be potentially found.”

The IAEA said in its confidential report circulated to member states last Tuesday and seen by The Associated Press that this new site contained “natural uranium metal in the form of fuel rods with cladding.” The agency verified the material and confirmed “the presence of around 73 tonnes of natural uranium metal.”

Grossi said when the inspectors visited the site in August they had to “tear down walls” and go through “very difficult and narrow passages” to reach the nuclear material that had been hidden. The site had “boxes scattered all over the place,” he said.
Grossi said that “the important thing is that this material now is under safeguards” of the IAEA, adding that agency inspectors had managed to install cameras at the location.

Asked if the nuclear material will remain in Syria or be removed, Grossi said that this is “a matter that the Syrian government will have to decide.” He added: “We are not requesting them to do this or to do that. For us what’s important is that we know all the time where this (material) is until the last gram.”

Logan Mintz, a director for nuclear materials security at the Washington-based Nuclear Threat Initiative, said that natural uranium metal is not directly usable for a nuclear weapon but it could be “diverted to a covert weapons program that further processes it into plutonium for a nuclear weapon.”

She said that once deemed safe to move, the material could be “transported in certified containers” to a third country that can “safely and securely disposition it into a more chemically stable and more widely used form” for possible use in nuclear power plants.
“As with any transport of nuclear material, this movement would require robust security from theft or sabotage,” she said.

title: A 9/11 widow reflects on 25 years of grief and what comes next
summary: "I felt this duty to give back, and I still do," Marian Fontana says.
story: When the 9/11 attacks unfolded, 25 years ago, most Americans remember exactly where they were at the moments hijacked planes crashed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and in a remote field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

Marian Fontana was in Brooklyn and had plans to celebrate her eighth wedding anniversary that day with her husband, Dave Fontana, a New York City firefighter. He stayed past his shift and like so many other firefighters, rushed to Lower Manhattan when the first plane struck, she said.
"And I dropped my son off for his second day of kindergarten," Marian Fontana said. "He was five. And I sat, I called [Dave] and said, 'you know, are you ready to go?'"
Fontana said there was a change of shifts around the time of the attack.
After the attacks, rows of media trucks were set up along West Side Highway, more than a mile from Ground Zero where first responders and crews searched for victims.

Frank Schramm, a professional photographer, says he grabbed his camera and began documenting scenes around the city. Looking back, he says it was one of the few ways to mark history before the era of smartphones and social media.
Reporters and photographers were often the "first witnesses of 9/11," he said, "and in a way they, by being there, were speaking to the world about what was going on."
For millions of Americans, the attacks were not something they experienced directly but witnessed on a TV screen. Regardless, the experience still left its mark.
Mindy Notheis says she was getting ready for work at her home in St. Louis, Missouri.

"And the first plane hit, there was tons of confusion and then the second plane hit and everybody knew that something was drastically wrong and then you just saw --within a matter of what, an hour? -- the towers fall," she said.

Notheis says she recently visited the 9/11 Memorial in Lower Manhattan with her niece -- who wasn't even born when the attacks happened -- paying their respects to the thousands of names inscribed in the bronze around the twin reflecting pools where the towers once stood.
She says she has made it a point to bring her other nieces and nephews to see the 9/11 Memorial and Museum over the years.
New York City, its residents and families who lost loved ones showed resilience in those initial days, weeks and months that followed.
After the attacks, relatives of victims, political leaders and the public have gathered at the 9/11 ceremonies in Lower Manhattan. But many other families have marked the anniversary in private.
Marian Fontana and her son, Aidan, who's now 30, say they will go to the beach to pay tribute to Dave.

"It's a mixed bag because I'm grateful that people remember, and yet sometimes it's really hard to go back there," Marian Fontana said. "It's very traumatic. And so I've really always let my son decide what we do on that day, and I think because it's been such a public event that we've been part of, he always chooses a very private."

Marian Fontana says after 25 years of raising her son and grieving, she can start thinking about what's next. She says that includes getting back to activities like comedy and writing, along with launching a podcast called "Firehouse Files," which features firsthand accounts from firefighters and first responders.

"I wanted to give back for the huge generosity that was shown to me after 9/11 and this overwhelming flow of generosity from the world," she said. "And I felt this duty to give back, and I still do. But there was a point at which I was kind of sacrificing my own, you know, my own well-being. So I'm kind of spending this next chapter kind of focusing on myself, returning to theater, returning to the things I love, and really trying to make this last chapter a happy one."
Michelle Franzen is a correspondent and anchor for ABC News and ABC Radio

title: Iran live updates: Saudi Arabia shuts down key pipeline after multiple attacks
summary: The Strait of Hormuz remains the primary flashpoint in the conflict.
story: Saudi Arabia said it shut down the East-West pipeline as a precautionary measure
President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28, with massive joint U.S.-Israeli strikes targeting military, government and infrastructure sites.
Delegations from the U.S. and Iran entered negotiations in June aimed at a war-ending deal based on a memorandum of understanding signed by both countries.

The U.S. and Iran have nonetheless continued to exchange strikes, with the strategic Strait of Hormuz as the primary flashpoint. Trump said in August that the U.S. would launch a "crushing economic operation" to force Tehran into submission.

Trump admin offering support to Saudi Arabia, but won't launch direct attacks in Yemen for now, officials say

The Trump administration is offering significant intelligence and targeting assistance to Saudi Arabia, but it does not currently plan on launching direct military attacks against the Houthis, two U.S. officials told ABC News.
Both officials cautioned that the administration’s thinking could change, particularly if the threat to Red Sea shipping lanes escalates significantly.

Saudi Arabian Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman spoke with President Donald Trump about the situation twice on Thursday, one official said, adding that the Saudi leader was seeking direct military intervention from the U.S. but that he did not indicate it was absolutely critical at this time.

"The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests -- such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea -- while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges,” a senior Trump administration official said when asked about the president’s calls with MBS. "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability.”

Another official said the Saudi government has communicated a willingness to launch a major military operation against the Houthis in recent days, even if it means going it alone, but that Riyadh had not yet made a final decision.

Both officials said that the Trump administration is continuing to closely monitor the situation in Yemen and that although assessments from earlier Friday indicated that the Houthis had taken control of the country’s west coast, Yemeni government forces and aligned militias were continuing to fight back and the situation could still change rapidly without outside intervention.

The Houthis (and their Iranian backers) are aware that attempting to choke off traffic in the Bab al-Mandeb would very likely trigger a stronger response from Saudi Arabia, the U.S. and potentially other countries. They have issued multiple statements indicating the strait is open to commercial traffic, but Houthi strikes on Saudi-linked ships have increased the risk level for all vessels, according to analysts.
-ABC News' Shannon K. Kingston
Saudi Arabia shuts down key pipeline after multiple attacks
Saudi Arabia announced it has shut down the East-West pipeline as a precautionary measure, saying it was subjected to multiple attacks on Thursday.
The attacks resulted in a number of injuries, according to Saudi Arabia.

An official source in the Ministry of Energy said "emergency teams and specialized technical crews initiated operations immediately following the attacks, taking the necessary procedures to secure the pipeline and verify its integrity in accordance with approved safety procedures and emergency response plans, in coordination with relevant authorities."
The East West pipeline goes from Saudia Arabia’s eastern oil fields, to the port of Yanbu in the west where oil can go to the rest of the world through the Bab al Mandeb strait.
This pipeline has been a critical means of mitigating the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran says it will meet with Gulf coast states on Monday

Iran claims that there will be a regional meeting with Gulf countries on Monday to discuss "the results of the negotiations between Iran and Oman regarding the establishment of safe routes for commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz," according to Iranian state TV, which cited Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei.

There has been no confirmation yet from the GCC countries on what states will be attending but the gathering, if it happens, would be the first meeting between the top diplomats from the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council and a senior Iranian official since the U.S. and Israel launched the war against the Islamic republic in February.
Trump touts war with Iran during 9/11 ceremony at Pentagon

During a speech at the Pentagon to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, Trump brought up the war with Iran as he discussed America's response to global terror in the quarter century since the attacks.

"For 25 years our best and bravest have kept America safe and today we salute every member of the United States military who served in the war on terror. It is a war on sick, horrible terror," he said.
"We salute the service members working right now to ensure the world's number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic republic of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon," he added.

title: Train derails in France and injures 44 as authorities investigate possible sabotage
summary: French authorities are investigating whether sabotage caused a train derailment in Normandy that injured 44 people
story: French authorities are investigating whether sabotage caused a train derailment in Normandy that injured 44 people

PARIS -- French authorities are investigating whether sabotage caused a train derailment that injured 44 people in Normandy, after a piece of rail was found on the track, police told The Associated Press on Saturday.
The regional train was carrying 186 passengers from Rouen to Caen when it derailed Friday evening at Cléon, in the Seine-Maritime department of northwestern France.
An 18-year-old woman was among the injured and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen University Hospital, police said.

A spokeswoman for the French national police communications service, known as SICOP, said that the piece of rail found on the track was “probably” linked to the derailment. She spoke on condition of anonymity because she wasn’t authorized to be publicly named in line with police policy.

Investigators were working to establish whether the circumstances were accidental or involved sabotage, the service said. The prosecutor’s office remained cautious about drawing conclusions, according to the police.
France’s previous rail disasters include the July 2013 derailment at Brétigny-sur-Orge, south of Paris, which killed seven people.
In November 2015, a high-speed TGV train carrying out tests derailed at Eckwersheim, near Strasbourg, killing 11.
More recently, a crash involving two high-speed trains at Adamuz in southern Spain killed 46 people and injured more than 100 in January, according to the Andalusian regional government.

title: Some 9/11 families call on Trump to hold Saudis accountable during NYC ceremony
summary: Some family members of 9/11 victims used the 25th anniversary ceremonies to openly call on the president to hold Saudi Arabia accountable for the attacks.
story: Family members openly called on the president to hold Saudi Arabia accountable.
Some family members of 9/11 victims used the 25th anniversary ceremonies to openly call on the federal government to hold Saudi Arabia accountable for the attacks.

During the ceremonial reading of the names at ground zero Friday, Terry Strada, the widow of 9/11 victim Tom Strada, received cheers after she admonished prior administrations, including the past presidents seated before her, for failing to get answers about the Saudi government's alleged role in the attacks.
"Administration after administration, including leaders in front of us here today, chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families," she said.

A coalition of victims' families are suing the Saudi government over their alleged role and have continued to pursue evidence they say points to deep Saudi complicity. The Saudis deny that claim and are fighting the suit in court.
Many of the 9/11 hijackers were Saudi nationals, according to the FBI.
The Saudis have repeatedly denied having any role in facilitating the attacks and replied in court that they remain "an ally of the United States [and] a sworn enemy of Al Qaeda."

White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told ABC News last week that "President Trump is leading the most transparent administration in history, and his team is working diligently to identify records that are responsive to these families' request."
Strada, the national chair of the advocacy group 9/11 Families United, said that presidential administrations broke "promises both public and private ... it has been one betrayal after another."
President Donald Trump "can still change that," she added.

"Tell the Saudis to stop lying," she said. "Tell them if they want to be friends with the USA they cannot continue to deny all of this -- all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through."
Trump attended a ceremony at the Pentagon at the time of the Manhattan ceremony. Strada urged Vice President JD Vance, who attended the ceremony, to "carry that message back" to Washington.
"How can it be, 25 years, and still we have no justice for the role Saudi Arabia played in your murder?" Strada asked as many attendees applauded in approval.
Strada wasn't the only family member who called on Trump to provide more scrutiny of the Saudi government.
A nephew of 9/11 victim Lisa Marie Terry also brought up the alleged Saudi involvement in the attacks after he finished reading some of the names.
"President Trump, you are our last hope. Release the unredacted files that implicate Saudi Arabia while what's left of the victims' families are still alive to see it," he said to cheers.

In statement released Friday afternoon, a White House spokesperson said, "President Trump is leading the most transparent administration in history, which is why he authorized the declassification and release of hundreds of pages of documents related to the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001."

"The President will always pay tribute to the American heroes we lost in the tragic September 11 attacks, their beautiful family members, and to the acts of heroism that defined that fateful day when the unbreakable spirit of the American people prevailed," the statement said.
On Friday, the CIA released 71 presidential briefs related to the 9/11 attacks, ranging in dates from 1998 to Sept. 12, 2001.

"The products trace the story of CIA analysts' evolving understanding of al-Qa'ida and efforts to highlight and warn of Osama Bin Ladin's attack plotting despite sparse, vague, and imperfect information," the agency said in a statement.

Brett Eagleson, the president of 9/11 Justice, the coalition of victims' families suing the Saudi government over its alleged role in the attacks, welcomed the documents' release but pointed out that the records omit key documents they've requested as part of their suit.

Most notably missing are phone records belonging to Omar al Bayoumi, a Saudi national, Eagleson said in a statement. According to a lawsuit filed by the some of the 9/11 families, Bayoumi allegedly provided logistical and financial support to two of the hijackers.
"Families have asked both past and current administrations to release the records that will help expose the full truth," Eagleson said.

"It is time for the Trump administration and Congress to do their part in helping the 9/11 Families get the justice we have fought for by holding the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia accountable for its proven role in the attacks that changed all of our lives so deeply and irreparably 25 years ago," he added.

In July, New York Republican Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, joined by Democratic Reps. Dan Goldman and Jerry Nadler, wrote a letter to a little-known but powerful advisory panel called the Public Interest Declassification Board, housed within the National Archives. It carries the power to consider requests for sensitive government secrets and make recommendations to the president about whether to declassify them.

The lawmakers' request, sent at the behest of the 9/11 families, bemoaned the "repeated obstacles" attorneys for the families have faced "in obtaining access to these materials from U.S. law enforcement and intelligence agencies."
Attorneys for the families believe those records could help them better understand the timing and nature of 9/11 hijackers' communications and key events in the hijackers' planning of the attacks.

The board responded weeks later, writing that it was "actively engaged in interagency consultations to determine what equities, if any, may remain in relation to these records." It urged patience as "those discussions continue."
The U.S. has long been a strategic partner with the Saudi Arabia for decades.

Trump has had a close relationship with the Saudi government in both of his terms and last November invited Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to the White House for a state visit. It was the first time MBS visited the U.S. in seven years.
Trump defended MBS when he was asked by ABC News chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce about the anger from 9/11 families over the visit.
"As far as this gentleman is concerned, he's done a phenomenal job," Trump said of the prince.
MBS responded, "I feel painful about families of 9/11 in America, but we have to focus on reality."
The prince alleged that Osama bin Laden used Saudis to destroy the relationship between the kingdom and the United States.
"We've been working to prove [bin Laden] wrong and continuing developing our nation. It is critical for the safety of the world," he said.
-ABC News' Cindy Smith and Nicholas Kerr contributed to this report.

title: Triplets carry on father's FDNY legacy after 9/11
summary: The triplet sons of an FDNY firefighter who responded to the Sept. 11 attacks are following in his footsteps and honoring the legacy he left behind.
story: A firefighter father's 9/11 sacrifice is inspiring his triplet sons to serve.
NEW YORK -- The triplet sons of an FDNY firefighter who responded to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks are not identical, but they share a common past and will soon share a common future.
They're three of the thousands of children who lost a parent 25 years ago on Sept. 11 or in the years after due to 9/11-related illnesses.

William Gormley's sons - Raymond, Billy and Kevin - were just 3 years old when their father rushed to the twin towers on Sept. 11, 2001. While many children lost parents that day, the brothers grew up with their father, only later learning the toll his work at Ground Zero had taken on his health.

"We all, for the most part, have the same lives in a lot of ways," Raymond said while sitting on a couch between his two brothers. "The same trauma, the same upbringing, the same everything. No one understands me like these two understand me."
But for Kevin, Raymond and Billy didn't learn about what happened from the history books, they lived it and they always had each other to rely on.
"This is a huge point my father always made, he said, 'These are your people. You were born with them, and this is what you got til the end,'" Kevin said.
They don't remember what happened on Sept. 11, since they were so young.
"Now, 25 years later, we're understanding the full grasp of what happened that day," Raymond said.
William Gormley rushed to the twin towers after they were struck. Unlike many children, they didn't lose their dad that day. The reality of the work he did hit later in life.
Firefighter Gormley worked on the pile for months, looking for survivors and later, for the remains of victims.
"It makes you feel some pride knowing your father went in there selflessly to help others and do the best he could," Kevin said.

The family said the long-term effects of his work became apparent over time. Growing up, the brothers accompanied their father to numerous doctor appointments but did not fully understand the severity of his health problems.
"They never really told us anything really," Billy said. "But as kids we'd go to hospital waiting rooms in summer for doctors' appointments. But not knowing the severity."

Raymond added, "Growing up he had skin cancer, sinus issues. So growing up as a kid, I personally never really understood what that came from. It wasn't until he was diagnosed with bladder cancer in 2016 that we put two together and realized it was from his time spent at Ground Zero."
William Gormley died of bladder and lung cancer in 2017. According to a report, he was one of more than 400 fire and EMS workers who have died from 9/11-related illnesses.
Asked whether his father would have made the same decision knowing what is now known about the dangers faced at Ground Zero, Raymond said there was no doubt.
"One hundred percent, without hesitation," he said. "Not only him, but every single person he went down with that day would go down to the pile again, without a doubt."
Today, a street in Brooklyn bears William Gormley's name, near the firehouse where he worked.
Despite their father's advice to seek work outside the fire service, the brothers found themselves drawn to the profession.
"My father would always say, 'When you get older, get a job where you sit behind a desk and write checks for people,'" Kyle said.
"He'd always say, 'Work with your brain, not your hands,'" Raymond added.

He went on to say, "So I'm a firefighter right now, an FDNY firefighter working at the same house he worked at, Ladder 174. So it's full circle really, it's crazy from him telling me to work with your brain, not your hands, and it's crazy I'm sleeping in the same bed he did 20 years ago."
Billy hopes to join the fire service soon.
"So I'm an EMT with the fire department at the moment," he said. "Waiting to join fire as well."
Kevin has also applied to become a firefighter.
"You hope one day, you can fill those shoes," he said.
The report said Billy and Kevin could join the fire academy as soon as this month.
The brothers said they were inspired not only by their father, but also by the support they received from firefighters after his death.

"Once I saw the camaraderie, everyone coming together, people driving us around, his old coworkers taking care of us, the laughs, the tears," Raymond said. "After that in my mind, it was something I would really like to do."
"Yeah, what they did was incredible how they took care of us, made sure everything was in order," another brother added.
And this didn't just have an impact on the three brothers, it impacted the entire family, including their big sister, Bridget.
"I think there's a beauty in that it was never forced down their throats," said Bridget. "My dad was never like, 'You're going to be a fireman!' Our dad was like, 'You're NOT going to be a fireman!'"

Bridget has also dedicated her work to preserving the stories of those affected by Sept. 11. She works with 9/11 survivors and produced a documentary about the dangers of toxic dust exposure. It's called, "Dust: Lingering Legacy of 9/11."
"Along the way, I got to know my father's friends better," she said. "I mean, I lost my dad, but I've got [sic] thousands of uncles now."

For the Gormley siblings, the events of Sept. 11 continue to shape their lives and careers. They say their shared experiences and bond have helped them navigate a loss that has defined much of their lives.
"Just being there for someone on their worst day, being their hope when there's no hope is really something special, something we take a lot of pride in," Raymond said.

"We all, for the most part, have the same lives in a lot of ways, the same trauma, the same upbringing, the same everything, no one understands me like these two understand me," one of the brothers said.
As they continue their careers in public service, the brothers say they are carrying forward the values their father exemplified, together.

title: Remembering the FDNY chaplain who raced to the Twin Towers on 9/11 to pray
summary: Twenty-five years after he rushed to help others on 9/11, FDNY Chaplain Father Mychal Judge's legacy of faith and compassion continues to inspire.
story: As chaos unfolded on Sept. 11 FDNY Chaplain Father Mychal Judge ran toward it.

NEW YORK -- FDNY Chaplain Mychal Judge raced to the twin towers on Sept. 11, 2001 from his midtown Engine Company One / Ladder Company 24. As the chaos unfolded, he prayed for the people trapped, for the rescuers and for humanity. His legacy of hope and service live on a quarter century after his death when the south tower collapsed.
"Today we will bury Mychal Judge," Father Michael Duffy said in a homily delivered after the chaplain's death. "We will bury his body, but not his spirit."
Judge, described as a close friend of Duffy and the first official victim of the 9/11 terror attacks, raced to the twin towers as the chaos unfolded.

"I pray for him every day," Duffy said. "And I think whenever there's excitement around or a fire truck or an ambulance or somebody need consolation, I think, 'Mychael Judge would be right there with them.'"

A French film crew happened to be profiling the FDNY that day and captured Father Judge's final moments inside the lobby of the north tower. He was praying for people jumping from the fire and smoke on the upper floors when the south tower collapsed, sending forth a tsunami of concrete and steel.
Duffy recalled learning of Judge's death while at his soup kitchen in Philadelphia.
"I had no doubt that when the plane hit the building, that he would be there," Duffy said.
An image of Judge's body being carried from the rubble became one of the enduring symbols of the attacks.

"That kind of is an icon that represents 2,000 people," Duffy said. "And the helplessness of goodness being overcome by evil and all those 2,000 people who died and how they were loved by their friends and families."
He went on to say, "I think that that picture symbolized it, that brought it concretely, that's why we feel empty."
The two men first met in the 1970s as Franciscan priests assigned to the same parish in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Duffy said Judge became a mentor without officially being a mentor.
Duffy also remembered Judge's humility.

"He had no airs about him, like he was better or standoffish," Duffy said. "So if you want to share what's really going on in your life, you want to gravitate to the most receptive person and that was him."

Born in Brooklyn, Judge shined shoes near the Church of St. Francis of Assisi on 31st Street before joining the Franciscan order. He was appointed FDNY chaplain in 1992 and ministered to people from all walks of life.
"There's another part of him that I don't know if too many people know that about him, he loved to be where the action was," Duffy said.
Four days after Judge's death, Duffy traveled to New York to deliver the homily at his funeral, as Judge had wanted. Thousands gathered at the church on 31st Street.
Even in death, Duffy said Judge left behind a message of service and compassion.
"We will bury his hands, but not his good works," said Duffy, repeating the lines from his homily at Judge's funeral. "We come to bury his heart, but not his love. Never his love."
Months after 9/11, Father Judge's gear and helmet were recovered. They are now on display at the New York City Fire Museum, alongside the FDNY memorial.

title: 25 years after 9/11, many first responders and survivors navigate health effects
summary: It’s estimated 400,000 people were exposed to toxins, risk of physical injury and stressful conditions from 9/11 and the aftermath, according to the WTC Health Program.
story: When Michael O'Connell found out he had been accepted into the New York City Fire Department, he was elated. O'Connell had started his career as a police officer, but he always had more of an interest in becoming a firefighter.
"It was more my speed," O'Connell told ABC News. "It was like camaraderie, team, unity. It's where I wanted to be."

O'Connell was sworn into the FDNY as a probationary firefighter. Just four months later, he was deployed to lower Manhattan on Sept. 11, 2001, following the terrorist attack at the World Trade Center.
For several weeks, O'Connell said he didn't go home. He went back-and-forth between his firehouse and ground zero, extinguishing fires amid the rubble and engaging in search-and-rescue operations.

O'Connell started hearing about fellow firefighters who worked at the site being diagnosed with asthma or cancer but didn't experience any health problems himself until New Year's Day 2007, when he says he woke up in severe pain.
"My body inflamed two times the size of what it was," O'Connell said. "I didn't know what was going on ... and I had like bruises and blisters all over my body."

O'Connell said he was eventually diagnosed with sarcoidosis, a multi-system inflammatory disease that typically affects the lungs, skin and lymph nodes, and his doctors believe is linked to his exposure to toxins at ground zero.

It's estimated that 400,000 people were exposed to toxic dust, smoke and debris; risk of physical injury; and physically and emotionally stressful conditions from 9/11 and the aftermath, according to the World Trade Center Health Program.

At least 69 cancers -- including breast, prostate, skin and head and neck -- have been certified as being linked to 9/11 as have airway and digestive disorders, musculoskeletal disorders and mental health conditions, according to the WTC Health Program.

More than 9,400 people have died from 9/11-related illnesses -- according to recently published data from the WTC Health Program -- which is three times higher than the 2,977 who died in the attacks in New York, at the Pentagon and in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Data from the WTC Health Program shows about 50,000 cancer diagnoses have been certified.

Many of these people are members of the FDNY and NYPD who responded to the attacks or assisted in cleanup operations, but they also include civilians -- those who lived, worked, went to school or passed through the area.

"The truth is, 9/11 didn't end on 9/11," Michael Barasch, managing partner at Barasch & McGarry, a law firm that specializes in helping 9/11 responders and survivors get compensation and health benefits, told ABC News. "I personally lost dozens of clients, mostly firefighters and police officers, on 9/11, but I have lost thousands of clients since."

"9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan," a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept. 11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live.
Responding to ground zero

On the morning of 9/11, Thomas Wilson, an NYPD sergeant, was investigating a burglary of an elderly couple in Brooklyn when calls came in over his radio that an object had hit the World Trade Center. Wilson replied that he was heading to the Williamsburg Bridge.
"I said goodbye to that couple, 'I'll come see you later on to take that report,'" Wilson told ABC News. "Never did see them again."

Wilson said he shut down the Williamsburg Bridge on the Manhattan side while his colleague shut down the Brooklyn side. The assignment went from facilitating the movement of vehicles over the bridge to securing it as people fled from Manhattan over the bridge on foot.
"I don't know how many thousands upon thousands of people crossed the bridge that day," Wilson said. "I'm still haunted. Covered in dust. ... That mass exodus out of Manhattan still sticks with me."
When O'Connell, the firefighter, got down to the site, he said he was instructed to help shut down the water mains, and then he climbed on the rubble to assist in search and rescue.

Throughout the day, O'Connell remembers hearing alarms. He said that attached to the Scott Air-Pak, a self-contained breathing apparatus that firefighters wear, is a Personal Alert Safety System (PASS) Alarm, which sits on the chest and tracks movement.
If a firefighter stays still for 20 to 30 seconds, it emits a loud beep to help colleagues locate them.

"That's all you heard were those alarms when we first got there. Nothing but PASS Alarms," O'Connell said. "As a fireman, when you hear it, you're meant to act and try your best to get to that person. You couldn't. They were underneath that pile."
John Feal, a demolition supervisor at ground zero who arrived on site on Sept. 12, also remembers the PASS Alarms going off.

"I don't care who you are, you're not programed ... to see that kind of devastation of that magnitude," he told ABC News. "I've never witnessed anything like that in my life, nor do I wish I ever see anything like that again."
Cleanup efforts

Wilson said he contributed to recovery efforts at ground zero, where he says he spent about 350 hours, and later as a sifter at Fresh Kills Landfill on Staten Island, which was temporarily reopened as a sorting ground for some of the ground zero rubble.
Wilson said he almost never thought about the dust and toxins he was inhaling.
"My mindset was just get the job done," Wilson said. "... Got to do what you got to do to keep things moving along."
At the landfill, Wilson said he was issued a disposable suit with boots, a hood, gloves and a respirator, but said the shifts were 12 hours, and that some respirator filters have an eight-hour limit.

Ivonne Sanchez, former FDNY emergency medical technician, arrived at ground zero after the towers fell and said she spent about 20 straight hours at the site. She said the dust was so thick that she couldn't get her bearings.

For the next several months, Sanchez worked on body identification and recovery efforts. She said she was motivated to continue responding at ground zero with the hope that she would find her friend, who died in the attacks.
Sanchez said she didn't receive a mask until October, when the site was visited by Occupational Safety and Health Administration inspectors for mandatory mask fittings.
O'Connell, the firefighter, said he didn't have a mask for the first few days until he received a painter's mask.

"You'd put them on but, quite honestly, you can't work with a painter's mask on for 24 hours straight and be a part of Bucket Brigade and talk to your guys and drink water," he said. "You're always pulling it on and off. Nobody was thinking, 'What's coming of this? Are we gonna get sick because we're breathing this stuff in?' That wasn't in anybody's head."
First responders begin falling ill
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said this week that more than 170,000 pages related to the attacks were being made public, including about air quality.

Among the documents revealed is the "Harding Memo," an October 2001 memo from then-Deputy Mayor Robert Harding that indicated the city knew of the air quality dangers and the legal liability, even though the city publicly declared the air was safe.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) also told the public at the time that the air around ground zero was safe to breathe. In an interview with The Guardian in 2016, Christine Todd Whitman, who was EPA administrator during 9/11, apologized for "whatever we got wrong" but denied that she knowingly lied about the air quality or knew at the time it was dangerous.

In Lower Manhattan, the collapse of the Twin Towers led to a massive dust cloud that filled the air and blanketed city blocks with ash, debris, metal, glass, asbestos, benzene and other harmful particles, according to the WTC Health program. Fires within the debris pile burned through the end of December 2001 with flare-ups in 2002.
The city did not immediately respond to ABC News' request on potential toxins first responders were exposed to in the aftermath or allegations by agencies at the time that the air was safe.

Medical research is ongoing about the potential links between 9/11-related toxic exposure and certain cancers and illnesses. Dozens of cancers and conditions have a certified link, but scientists are still learning about the cumulative effects of breathing in a "toxic cocktail," how long it may take for certain cancers to develop -- if they do at all -- and how chemical exposure and trauma can accelerate physical decline and life expectancy.

Sanchez, the EMT, said she would often go home after a day at ground zero coughing, bleeding from her nose or vomiting. Sanchez retired in 2002 after recovery efforts ended due to an injury at the site, which she said caused lower back pain and nerve damage that she said she manages to this day.

In the years after 9/11, Sanchez said she developed chronic sinusitis and asthma. In 2014, in her early 40s, she said she began experiencing severe hot flashes. Sanchez said she went to the doctor four weeks later and was diagnosed with breast cancer that spread to her lymph nodes.
"It was Stage II and ... it was very aggressive," Sanchez said.

Sanchez said she had a lumpectomy in August 2014 and a mastectomy in December 2014. While Sanchez says her cancer is currently in remission, she said she has also developed seven or eight stomach ulcers that have caused gastrointestinal problems from her time at ground zero.

Wilson, the police officer, said he also developed cancer. Wilson was diagnosed with an aggressive neck cancer that had spread to his tongue and skeletal muscle after going to the doctor for sinus issues and tongue pain, he said.
Wilson said he underwent a procedure called a hemiglossectomy, which involved removing part of his tongue, along with a neck dissection to remove the neck tumor and 39 lymph nodes.
Doctors used a skin graft from the wrist to replace part of Wilson's tongue as well as an artery from his arm to implant in his neck, he said.

To this day, Wilson said he continues to take medication for his thyroid, experiences fibrosis in his neck, attends swallow therapy and sleeps with an oxygen machine due to severe asthma. He said he also suffers from osteoradionecrosis in his jaw, a serious condition in which bone dies after being exposed to radiation therapy.
Wilson said he also started seeing a mental health specialist two years ago.
"I had a lot to unpack," he said. "It eases me and it helps me get back, and I know I had a lot of anxiety; I still do."
O'Connell, the firefighter, learned he had developed sarcoidosis when his wife was pregnant with the couple's first child, he said.

"I just [thought], this is the first child I'm gonna have. Maybe the only. I just want to get to that day. Get me to the day so I can see this baby and see you and her together, and then I'm good," O'Connell said.

O'Connell said he received drugs, including cancer medications and steroids as treatment. He said he was told there was never a case of sarcoidosis in the history of the FDNY until he was diagnosed but, since then, there have been many more cases, according to O'Connell.
O'Connell returned to work but said he had to retire as a lieutenant in 2010 after experiencing flare-ups while he was in the line of duty.
"That's your family. ... It's a house of 50 guys, and we do everything together," he said. "It's a family and leaving that is one of the worst things that's ever happened in my life."
Many first responders have died from their illnesses, including William Gormley, a firefighter with the New York City Fire Department.

His daughter, Bridget Gormley, said from 9/11 until his death, he had a persistent cough. She said her father was also riddled with skin cancer following his time at ground zero and was going to the doctor two or three times a year to remove cancerous tissue from several areas including his back, arms and nose.
In Christmas 2016, William Gormley was diagnosed with bladder cancer. The cancer spread to his lungs, and he died in June 2017.

"I think my father was well aware that it was caused from being downtown, ground zero, in the pit, in a pile," Bridget Gormley told ABC News. "He and his friends would joke, 'This is all going to kill us one day.' Very gallows humor, but I think they knew."
"I couldn't wrap my head around it': Civilians develop illnesses as well
9/11-related illnesses didn't just affect the first responders but also civilians, including people who were working in the area at the time.

Barbara Mohan, office administrator and paralegal at Barasch & McGarry, said she first realized something was wrong in 2016, when she tripped on an uneven sidewalk walking across City Hall Park on her way to the office and fell on her knee.
Mohan said she went to a hospital, where doctors determined she hadn't broken or fractured any bones. Within a week or two, Mohan said she started to get pain in her hip.

She said she went to an orthopedist, who diagnosed her with bursitis -- inflammation of a small fluid-filled sac that cushions the bones, tendons and muscles near joints -- and recommended physical therapy.

"The more I went to physical therapy, the more it hurts," Mohan told ABC News. "Another X-ray, and then [the orthopedist] sent me for an MRI, and it showed a lesion on my hip bone, kind of the top of the femur."

The doctor referred Mohan to Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, she said, where she was diagnosed with large B-cell lymphoma, a subtype of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma that affects the lymphatic system.

Mohan, who had been working in an office just blocks away from the World Trade Center since 1996 -- and returned to work three weeks later -- was told by colleagues at the firm that they believed her cancer was linked to her 9/11 exposure.
"I just couldn't wrap my head around it," she said. "I just got cancer. I guess I never associated it to [9/11] ever, not once. And I work here, two blocks away."

Barasch, the attorney, said he also developed cancer. In 2018, he was diagnosed with prostate cancer, which is the second most common cancer in the 9/11 community, and then years later, he was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma, a skin cancer, when doctors noticed irregular coloring under his thumb.

"Of course, I knew right away it was caused by my exposure," Barasch said. "I was here on 9/11, caught in the dust cloud, moved back three weeks later. ... So, I knew, because this is what I do for a living, I suspect the average civilian has no idea."
The fight for benefits

Feal, the demolition supervisor, said he was injured at ground zero on Sept. 17, 2001, when a falling piece of steel landed on his left foot. He said he developed gangrene, then sepsis, and eventually required a partial amputation.

He said he was denied compensation from the first 9/11 Victims' Compensation Fund (VCF) created by Congress because his injury occurred outside of a 96-hour window of eligibility for rescue workers. Feal was injured about 123 hours after the attack.

A spokesperson for the VCF told ABC News that questions about denied compensation under the first VCF "should be directed to those who implemented the program and formulated the regulations," and pointed to remarks VCF Special Master Allison Turkel provided during a press briefing last week.

The denial spurred Feal to become an advocate for 9/11 first responders. Feal founded the FealGood Foundation to help ground zero workers receive assistance, spread awareness and advocate, including lobbying members of Congress.

"I had nothing to prove. I had a documented injury," Feal said. "All of those men and women, uniform and non-uniform, and those people that [went] to work, that went to school in lower Manhattan, they had to prove they got sick from 9/11."

Feal and several first responders suffering from 9/11-related illnesses lobbied Congress in the late 2000s to help pass the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act of 2010, which provides health monitoring and aid to the first responders, volunteers and survivors of the attacks. This also led to the establishment of the WTC Health Program.

James Zadroga was an NYPD officer who responded to recovery efforts at ground zero and died in 2006 of a respiratory disease. Two separate autopsies reportedly linked his death to inhaling toxic substances at ground zero and he was the first NYPD officer whose death was attributed to exposure at the site.
Turkel said during the press briefing last week that the VCF has received more than 112,000 claims and has awarded more than $18.56 billion to over 77,000 claimants since reopening in 2011.

The Zadroga Act expired in 2015, and Feal and first responders went down again to Washington, D.C. O'Connell, the firefighter, testified before Congress, as did late night host Jon Stewart in a clip that went viral.
"What Jon did in those eight-and-a-half, nine minutes in front of Congress that America saw really moved the needle," Feal said.
In December 2015, the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Reauthorization Act passed, which extended medical benefits to affected individuals until 2090.
25 years later

The first responders -- O'Connell, Wilson and Sanchez -- often conduct outreach, including speaking at schools, sharing with students their experiences at Ground Zero and their work to ensure first responders receive health care and compensation.

"I think [9/11 is] an historical event, but also, we're still living with ... many of the repercussions that happened that day," Wilson said. "So, I would like to see more schools make sure they're teaching about it."

The 9/11 Memorial & Museum announced earlier this year it will add a seventh moment of silence and a bell toll at this year's 25th commemoration ceremony to honor those who have died of illnesses related to their time at or near the World Trade Center site.

For the past 24 years, there have been six moments of silence followed by bell tolls: two to mark the times when the planes struck the World Trade Center towers; one to mark when a plane struck the Pentagon; one to mark when a plane crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania; and two to mark the collapses of the Twin Towers.
Knowing what they know now, and having suffered their various illnesses, O'Connell, Wilson and Sanchez all said they would respond to ground zero the way they did a quarter-century ago.
"I wouldn't change a thing," O'Connell said. "I can't say anything else but that. Nothing, not a thing."

title: Students with President Bush on 9/11 look back on day: 'You could see it on his face'
summary: Students of Emma E. Booker Elementary School in 2001 remember watching President George W. Bush react to 9/11.
story: Former Sarasota, Florida, second grade student Krystal Davis remembers a wave of confusion washing over her and her classmates on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, after a suited man whispered into the ear of the president of the United States, who was seated just in front of the students.

Then-President George W. Bush was visiting Emma E. Booker Elementary School and had been listening intently to the children in Mrs. Sandra Daniels' second-grade class flexing their reading skills, when the look of admiration on his face suddenly gave way to an expression of concern.

Chief of Staff Andrew Card had just relayed to Bush that a second plane had crashed into the World Trade Center in New York City. "America is under attack," he later recalled whispering to the president.

9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan,” a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live.

"You could see the shift with [the president] once he got the message, and then you could see it on his face," Davis said in an interview with ABC News commemorating 25 years since the 9/11 attacks. "And then the shift of him going back to his normal self and smiling like, 'I don't want to alarm the kids.'"
Teacher Daniels told Sarasota ABC affiliate WWSB in an interview published Tuesday that she "immediately knew something was wrong" at that moment.
"His entire demeanor changed," she recalled, referring to Bush.
Davis described the concern among the students as Bush was escorted out of the room, once the reading lesson concluded.
"And we're just like, 'OK, in the middle of reading, what happened? What did we do? Like, did we do something wrong? Did he not like us reading or whatever?'" Davis recalled.
Though unaware at the time, Davis and her classmates had a front-row seat to history.

Meanwhile, 10-year-old Stevenson Tose'-Rigell, son of principal Gwendolyn Tose'-Rigell, was in the school's library eagerly awaiting the president's arrival, where Bush was slated to deliver a speech on his signature education policy, the No Child Left Behind Act.
"I'd probably say it was a couple of hours at least we were out there on the podium waiting around. We didn't know what was going on at the time," he said.

He continued, "They were trying to entertain us a little bit and, you know, keep, everybody feeling kind of excited … but we're waiting around for hours, you know, it's like, 'Man, this is this a long time waiting around for someone.'"

Tose'-Rigell said Bush did eventually enter the room, but the 10-year-old quickly realized the speech Bush was delivering would not touch on education policy. Instead, Bush delivered an address to the nation, confirming reports of "an apparent terrorist attack on our country."
"We're pretty much [thinking], 'Sounds like we're under attack,'" Tose'-Rigell recalled. "So yeah, it was definitely far off from the script."
Back in Daniels' classroom, Davis said the children were moved into another room, where a teacher tried to explain what was going on.
Davis said it was at that moment the students watched the images of the World Trade Center's Twin Towers crashing down on a television.
Tose'-Rigell said he was not able to leave school right away, as his mother was the school's principal. Instead, he said he watched the devastation unfold on a small TV in the school's front office.
From Sarasota, Bush boarded Air Force One, departing Florida for military bases in Louisiana and Nebraska before arriving back in Washington, D.C., that night.

By day's end, nearly 3,000 people had died in terror attacks at the World Trade Center in New York City; the Pentagon building in Arlington, Virginia; and in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, the crash site of United Airlines Flight 93.
A quarter century later, as the country continues to grapple with the ramifications of that day, so too do the alumni of Emma E. Booker Elementary who were at the school the day of the attacks.

In May, the school commemorated the 25th anniversary of 9/11 by welcoming a steel beam from the World Trade Center, brought by the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, which allows the public to "put their hand on that steel and feel the loss and sacrifice that was made that day."

Stephen Siller Jr., whose father Stephen Siller was one of the 343 New York City Fire Department members killed on 9/11, said bringing the steel beam to Emma E. Booker Elementary was one of the most impactful visits he's made with the foundation's Steel Across America campaign, out of dozens of similar trips.
"Little kids ... understand that, you know, this is a sacred piece of history," he said. "...It once held up the Twin Towers, it once held floors and walls, and now it holds the gravity of that day."
In a statement to ABC News, Sarasota County Schools Superintendent Terry Connor reflected on the impact 9/11 had on the district.
"For Sarasota County Schools, the legacy of Sept. 11 carries a uniquely personal connection," the statement read in part.
It added, "On this 25th anniversary, we honor those who were lost, remember those who answered the call, and express our gratitude to all who continue to serve our communities and our country."

Speaking with ABC News, the former students of Emma E. Booker Elementary reflected on their intersection with history, recognizing the grave impact on those directly affected by the tragedy while also considering the mark it left on their own lives.

"You realize, 'People really lost they live[s] yesterday,'" Davis said, recounting the days following 9/11. "And we were right in the midst of everything. [The president] was right here in Sarasota, Florida, [when it happened]."
Davis, who currently works in healthcare but said she aspires to be a police officer, said the events that day inspired her to pursue a career serving others.

"As a second grader, I couldn't really explain," Davis said, adding that she would later realize her experience left her "wanting to do more for my community, wanting to do more for myself and my kids."
"That day is going to always be something I never forget," she added.
Tose'-Rigell said he also carries complex feelings surrounding his memory of that day, including sadness and a sense of pride.
His mother, the school's former principal, died in 2007 after a battle with cancer.

"I always knew my mom was a rock star, you know? In my mind, you know, she was my superhero," Tose'-Rigell said, describing seeing his mother on the world stage on Sept. 11, 2001, and the "national recognition" she received.
He added that seeing her in archival footage from that day brought back memories of her each year on the anniversary of 9/11.
"It feels like she comes back," he said. "You know, like, once a year, [she] reincarnates right onscreen again."

title: 9/11 firefighter's son spends months bringing steel from World Trade Center across US
summary: Stephen Siller Jr. spent the last four months bringing a 16,900-pound steel beam from the World Trade Center to dozens of cities across the U.S.
story: On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, 34-year-old New York City firefighter Stephen Siller had just finished his overnight shift when he heard a call come in on the scanner.
"He immediately knew something was awry," so he drove to his firehouse in Brooklyn, his son, Stephen Siller Jr., told ABC News.

"When he got there, he realized his whole unit had responded [to the World Trade Center]," Siller Jr. said. "So he grabbed his gear, threw it in his truck and started to make his way to the World Trade Center. But on 9/11, they shut down every entryway into Manhattan."
He parked his car by the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel, Siller Jr. said, put about 60 pounds of gear on his back, and ran through the tunnel to the South Tower of the World Trade Center.

Stephen Siller was among 343 New York City Fire Department members killed on 9/11. He was survived by his close-knit siblings, his wife Sally, and his five children, including Stephen Jr., who was 9 months old.

Siller Jr., now 25, doesn't have his own memories of his father, but he's poured his energy into honoring those who died on 9/11. And to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks, he spent the last four months bringing a 16,900-pound steel beam from the World Trade Center to dozens of cities across the U.S. in hopes that seeing a piece of history up close will help Americans remember, learn and be inspired.

The Steel Across America campaign allows the public to "put their hand on that steel and feel the loss and sacrifice that was made that day -- the sacrifice of first responders and their loss, the loss of innocent people who just went to work," Stephen Siller Jr.'s uncle, Frank Siller, told ABC News.

"9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan," a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live.
Siller Jr. described the entire tour as "incredibly powerful."

At the first stop, ground zero, a firefighter whose entire unit was killed on 9/11 "walked up to the steel and he put his hand on it, and he was overcome with emotion," Siller Jr. recalled. "You could just immediately see tears rushing down his face. And he started to hug the steel like he was hugging his friends he lost 25 years ago."
To Siller Jr., the steel represents the more than 1,000 bodies never recovered from the World Trade Center -- including his father's.
"Who they are is ingrained in that steel, what they did is ingrained in that steel. It holds the memory of that day," he said. "It's the most overwhelming piece of history I've ever come across."

The beam represents "resilience, strength, but also sacrifice," Frank Siller added. "... Ground zero is my brother's burial place, obviously. But the steel has his -- embodies his soul, and the souls of so many."

As Siller Jr. spent his summer traveling the U.S., from Oklahoma to California to Mount Rushmore in South Dakota, he said he was surprised by how many people had personal connections to the terror attacks, like the police officer he met in Seattle whose uncle was killed on 9/11.

"And we had thousands of people show up to 35 events across the country who may not have had a connection to 9/11," he added, "but for them, they wanted to mourn that day, they wanted to make sure they never forgot."

"Everywhere we went was incredible -- the support, it was mind-boggling," Siller Jr. said. "In Texarkana, a small, little town in Texas, we had about 1,000 people show up to an event. It was unbelievable. You know, companies letting all their employees out of work to go see this piece of steel."
