title: US restricts government travel to Mexican border city over threat concerns
summary: The U.S. Consulate in Nogales announced restricted government travel to essential daylight movement only over an unspecified threat in Sonora, Mexico.
story: Fox News correspondent Madison Scarpino reports on allegations that cartels are smuggling fuel from the United States into Mexico as the illicit trade becomes a major source of revenue for criminal organizations on ‘The Will Cain Show.’
Travel restrictions have been placed on U.S. government employees in the Mexican border city of Nogales, Sonora, according to officials.
The U.S. Embassy and Consulates in Mexico on Saturday issued a warning restricting government activity over an unspecified threat in Nogales, Sonora, in Mexico.

"Due to threat information, U.S. government activities in, and travel to, Nogales have been restricted to essential movement during daylight hours only," the U.S. Consulate General in Nogales said in a statement.
STATE DEPARTMENT URGES AMERICANS TO AVOID MEXICAN CITY JUST ACROSS TEXAS BORDER
The U.S. Embassy and Consulates in Mexico on Saturday issued a warning restricting government activity over an unspecified threat in Nogales, Sonora, in Mexico. (Getty Images)
"We are alerting U.S. citizens of this threat and change in posture," the statement continued.

Sonora's State Security Board said it contacted U.S. consular officials after the alert was issued but did not provide information identifying a specific threat. State authorities said they had no information establishing a concrete risk to the public, though they would continue preventive security operations in Nogales.
The alert also reminded Americans that the U.S. Travel Advisory designates Sonora as a Level 3 "Reconsider Travel" area.

Anyone in the area is urged to exercise increased caution and be aware of their surroundings, seek shelter in the event of an incident, notify friends and family of their safety in the event of an incident, follow instructions from Mexican law enforcement, and monitor local media for updates.
The alert reminded Americans that the U.S. Travel Advisory designates Sonora as a Level 3 "Reconsider Travel" area. (Getty Images)
U.S. lawmakers also encouraged people in the area to pay attention to the warnings issued by the U.S. government.
"For Americans in or near Nogales - or who may have family members or friends there: please heed the guidance and warnings from the U.S. government," Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz., said on X.
"We are praying for the safety of U.S. citizens and personnel who may be in harm's way," he added.
AMERICANS WARNED POPULAR TRAVEL ROUTES THIS SUMMER COULD CARRY CRIME AND KIDNAPPING RISKS
Rep. Andy Biggs encouraged people in the area to pay attention to the warnings issued by the U.S. government. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
It remains unclear what threat in Nogales triggered the security warning.

title: Germany’s far-right party AfD surges to historic victory in state election
summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's party faces a disastrous blow as AfD aims for Germany's first far-right state government since World War II.
story: Far-left primary victories signal a shift as lifelong Democrat Jamie Metzl urges party leaders to reject Democratic Socialists of America candidates. Metzl highlights Angie Nixon’s Florida primary win, where she defeated her opponent despite being outspent, as a warning sign. He argues that maintaining a moderate, patriotic two-party system is essential for American democracy.

The far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD) was projected to win a strong victory in a regional election on Sunday, in a major blow to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right party, the Christian Democratic Union.
Merz's party was projected to be hit with a disastrous result in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
AfD had sought to form the country’s first far-right state government since the end of World War II in 1945, although it was not immediately clear whether it would be able to fulfill that ambition.
Ulrich Siegmund, AfD's anti-migration candidate for governor, said that "we have written history."
ANTI-MIGRANT AFD SEEKS TO BREAK GERMANY'S POLITICAL 'FIREWALL' IN HISTORIC STATE ELECTION

Top candidate Ulrich Siegmund shows thumbs up beside party leaders Tino Chrupalla and Alice Weidel, from left, at an AfD election party after the Saxony-Anhalt state elections. (AP Photo/Matthias Schrader)
Siegmund, 35, told public broadcaster ARD that voters had sent a message that "things cannot carry on like this," adding that it was "also a signal toward Berlin."
"A very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz. Every day this man is in the chancellery is one too many," he said of Germany's unpopular leader.
The election comes amid widespread public discontent with the national government, which has yet to convince many voters it can get the country's sluggish economy back on track.

AfD aimed for an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern on its own and overcome the so-called firewall of mainstream parties’ refusal to work with it. But it was unclear long after polls closed whether that goal would become reality.

"AfD is a right-wing extremist party. It wants to leave the euro; that would be economic downfall ... it works closely together with Russia, it wants a completely different social model," said Franziska Hoppermann, the national general-secretary of Merz's party. "We will not work with them."
Achieving its first state government would be the biggest victory in the anti-migration party’s 13-year history.

Regardless of whether AfD forms its own government, the projected result is still a blow to Merz, whose center-right party has led Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years. Unlike several other European countries, modern Germany has not had a far-right or right-wing populist party leading a national, state or major-city government.

After the projections for the state election in Saxony-Anhalt were released, members of various coalitions protested against the AfD on the Römer, holding a sign that read "Anti-social, fascist, stupid!!!" (Boris Roessler/dpa via AP)
AfD is the largest opposition party in Germany’s national parliament and is strongest in the formerly communist and less prosperous east, where Saxony-Anhalt sits.

Its regional branch in Saxony-Anhalt is one of several classified as a confirmed right-wing extremist group by the domestic intelligence agency, which cites members' disparagement of migrants from Muslim countries, among other things.
The party promotes "remigration," which pushes for the deportation of immigrants.

Siegmund has said his top priorities include "a deportation offensive" and ending incentives for people to come to Germany and "exploit our social system." He also wants to initiate a process to pull Saxony-Anhalt from the regional public broadcaster over allegations of "disinformation."
Germany’s 16 states have extensive powers, including overseeing security matters and running the education system.
An AfD leader in a neighboring state appealed two convictions for knowingly using a Nazi slogan.
The party has pushed back on accusations of extremism as politically motivated.
GERMANY BLAMES RUSSIA AFTER EXPLOSIVE-LADEN DRONE FOUND NEAR UKRAINIAN CARGO PLANES AT MAJOR AIRPORT
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Saxony-Anhalt State Governor and top candidate Sven Schulze give a press statement after visiting UPM Biochemicals in Leuna, Germany. (AP Photo/Matthias Schrader)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Projections for ARD and ZDF public television, based on exit polls and partial counting, have AfD at just over 44% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin.

Merz's Christian Democratic Union was significantly behind, polling 18% and losing about half its support. The Left Party, the center-left Social Democrats and Greens were seen polling around 9% each.
It was unclear whether the BSW party would reach the 5% of the vote needed to win seats. The projections put AfD at least marginally short of an absolute majority for now, but that could change.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Saudi shutdown of key pipeline limits oil flow as Yemen hits back against Houthis
summary: Saudi Arabia has closed a critical oil pipeline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq, the latest squeeze on Middle Eastern supplies after attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels this week threatened to deepen the world’s energy crisis.
story: Saudi Arabia has closed a critical oil pipeline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq, the latest squeeze on Middle Eastern supplies after attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels this week threatened to deepen the world’s energy crisis.

The 745-mile pipeline had helped Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest crude oil exporter, bypass the blocked Strait of Hormuz, through which some 20% of the world’s oil used to pass before the U.S. and Israel waged war on Iran in late February.

The Saudi Energy Ministry confirmed the shutdown of the East-West pipeline on Friday, adding that drone attacks had resulted in a number of injuries and that its teams were “taking the necessary measures to secure the pipeline and assess its safety.”

Saudi Arabia said it would not retaliate for now following a request from Iraq’s prime minister, while reserving the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security and critical facilities, according to a Saudi foreign ministry statement.
The pipeline has been moving 4-5% of global oil supplies, new agency Reuters reported Friday.

An Iraqi military commander was dismissed early on Saturday after investigations confirmed the latest drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia originated from Iraq, according to a statement by Iraq‘s prime minister’s office.
Iraq also closed two key border crossings with Iran, Iraq’s state-run news agency reported Saturday.

Kuwait, a U.S. ally in the region, warned that the pipeline attack was a “dangerous escalation that undermines the security and stability of the region,” while Bahrain stressed Saudi Arabia’s right to “take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty.”

U.S. President Donald Trump said on ⁠Saturday that everything would “work out just ⁠fine” when asked about the region on a visit to Ireland. He also said, without providing evidence, that Iran was “probably” behind the pipeline attack.

The pipeline strikes came as rebel Houthi forces in Yemen captured Perim, an island in the middle of the vital Bab el Mandeb Strait, which serves as a gateway to the Red Sea trade route that links Europe and Asia.

The Houthis also captured the historic port city of Mocha this week, followed by an advance on the strategic coastal town of Dhubab and the apparent withdrawal of forces from the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government from Perim, also known as Mayun.

If the Houthis are able to threaten shipping along the Bab el Mandeb Strait, it could reduce oil supplies through another key waterway. Saudi Arabia has had to rely on the Red Sea route given the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz.
Yemeni Ministry of Defense said Saturday it had carried out counterattacks against Houthi targets, hitting militants, vehicles and weaponry.

A statement issued by Houthi forces on Friday said that “maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels,” vowing to strike Saudi targets “until the aggression stops and the blockade against our dear people is lifted.”
Trump said the Houthis had contacted the U.S. to stress that they “don’t want to fight with us” and would “much prefer not having us involved.”
Oil prices ended the week above $100 a barrel for the first time since Mid-May after the dramatic developments.

Effective Houthi control over the Red Sea coast “is a game changer,” and could give Iran powerful new leverage in its war with the United States, Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics, told NBC News.
He said: “Far from being really besieged and bleeding, Iran now could easily increase the pain to the U.S. economy and the world economy.”
Gerges said it remains to be seen whether the Houthis can maintain their control of the vast areas of the Red Coast, or if they “overextended themselves.”

But the Trump administration “now finds itself in a much more difficult position because it gambled that the blockade of Iran would force Iran to accept Trump’s conditions,” he added. “The reverse has happened.”

Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian said Saturday that it would sign an agreement with Oman over a joint route through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, as part of a deal securing future navigation rights through the strait.
That deal is not expected to immediately reopen the waterway without a broader agreement with the U.S., Iran has previously stressed.

The U.S. military is helping its Saudi counterparts to develop and coordinate targets inside Yemen, according to a U.S. official and a person familiar with the matter, after Saudi Arabia vowed a firm response to hostilities.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman is urging President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, according to a person familiar with the matter. The president and the Crown Prince have discussed the recent escalation by the Houthis at least twice in the last 24 hours, this person said Friday.
The United Nations’ International Organization for Migration warned on Friday at least 46,000 people have so far been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week.
It said that figure spanned the West Coast and Taiz governorates as of Thursday, with the numbers of those displaced “alarmingly rising by the hour.”
The organization called on all parties to the conflict to “guarantee safe humanitarian access and to protect civilians, aid workers and assets on the ground.”

title: Your health insurance bills are about to go up
summary: Most Americans can expect to pay significantly more each month for health insurance next year, whether they get it through work, Obamacare or Medicare.
story: Most Americans can expect to pay significantly more each month for health insurance next year, whether they get it through work, Obamacare or Medicare. In some cases, the premium increases may be the largest in decades and are driven by numerous economic pressures. But they won’t look the same for everyone. Some will pay more in the form of higher copays or deductibles.

“Healthcare costs are going up faster than they have in years, and open enrollment is when the healthcare affordability crisis is really going to hit home for people,” said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF, a nonpartisan research group. “That’s true for whatever kind of insurance you have.”
Prices have shifted upward in every corner of daily life.

The rising healthcare costs stem in part from higher prices for hospital and other medical care, as well as the increased use of expensive prescription drugs — including GLP-1 weight loss medications — that are driving up spending for insurers and employers.
The pressures are unique to each type of coverage.

People who buy insurance through the Affordable Care Act marketplace, about 19 million adults, are set to face another year of steep premium increases after the enhanced federal subsidies expired last year.

On Thursday, the White House promised $500 rebate checks to an estimated 1 million ACA enrollees, alleging they were wrongly overcharged. It’s unclear where the money for the rebates would come from or whether the distribution would require approval from Congress, but experts say it’s unlikely to provide significant relief.

The $500 check “pales in comparison to the increased premiums that marketplace enrollees are facing due to the expiration of the enhanced subsidies,” said Miranda Yaver, an assistant professor of health policy and management at the University of Pittsburgh.

Workers with job-based insurance may be asked to shoulder more of their employers’ rising health costs. And some Medicare beneficiaries could see changes to their prescription drug premiums after the Trump administration ended a temporary program that helped keep those premiums in check.
Here’s what to expect.
The Affordable Care Act
People who buy health insurance through the ACA are on track for a second straight year of double-digit premium increases.

Insurers who offer ACA plans are proposing a premium increase of about 15%, on average, for 2027, according to a KFF analysis of public filings from insurers across all 50 states and Washington, D.C. For 2026, insurers upped rates by an average of 20%.

An individual earning $80,000 a year who doesn’t qualify for standard ACA subsidies could see the cost of their bronze plan — the cheapest plan — rise by roughly $80 a month, adding almost $1,000 to their annual tab.

One of the biggest reasons insurers are hiking rates is that medical care is getting more expensive, Levitt said. Insurers have pointed to higher prices for hospital stays, doctor’s visits and prescription drugs, among other costs.
Insurers generally “have felt pressure to add coverage of GLP-1 drugs for weight loss, but they’re also seeing big, big increases in costs for those drugs,” Levitt said.

The ACA marketplace is also still adjusting to the expiration of the enhanced federal subsidies at the end of 2025. Those subsidies — first put in place during the pandemic — lowered monthly premiums for millions of people in the middle class. When they expired, people either paid significantly more for coverage in 2026 or downgraded their plans.
The expired subsidies also led ACA enrollment to fall by about 3 million.

Young adults — who are generally healthier and more likely to go without insurance when it becomes too expensive — accounted for a large portion of the enrollment decrease. That left insurers with a group of customers who, on average, need more medical care, Yaver said,  which was also factored into insurers rates for 2027.
Job-based health insurance
Most Americans, about 165 million people, get health insurance through their jobs. Many of them may be feeling the price increases, too.

Employers expect the cost of providing health benefits to each worker to rise 8.2%, on average, in 2027 — the largest increase since 2003, according to a survey of more than 1,800 employers by Marsh, a benefits consulting group.

That doesn’t necessarily mean workers’ premiums will rise by 8.2%, said Dr. Kevin Schulman, a professor of medicine at the Stanford University School of Medicine who researches employer-based health insurance.

Employers typically subsidize a large portion of workers’ health coverage. But when healthcare  costs rise too sharply, Schulman said, employers have several ways of passing some of the increase along to employees. They can charge workers more for their monthly premiums, raise deductibles or make other changes to their benefits.
Sometimes, they slow wage increases to offset the expense.

“Because the costs are going up, the employers are trying to reduce the rate of growth, and the easiest way to reduce the rate of growth of healthcare costs is to push more of the costs onto the employee,” Schulman said.
Many appear prepared to do just that.
The Marsh survey found about two-thirds of large employers — those with 500 or more employees — said they expected to increase how much employees contribute toward their premiums in 2027.

Others may shift costs in other ways, including waiving copays and deductibles for primary care visits while charging for other kinds of care, or keeping premiums the same while raising the deductible.

For workers, that makes it important to look beyond the premium during open enrollment, Schulman said. A plan that costs less or about the same each paycheck may come with a higher deductible or require people to pay more when they seek care.
Medicare
Monthly premiums are handled somewhat differently for the roughly 70 million people enrolled in Medicare.

People on Medicare generally have more than one premium to consider: typically, a premium for Part B, which covers doctor’s visits and other outpatient care; and, for 9 out of 10 enrollees, a separate premium for Part D, which covers prescription drugs.
Prescription drug costs are where enrollees may see the biggest changes, according to Yaver, of the University of Pittsburgh.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projected in July that the baseline monthly cost for Part D coverage will rise about 6% in 2027, from $38.99 to $41.33.
What enrollees actually end up paying varies, depending on their income and their specific plan.

The increase stems from the Trump administration withdrawing its support for a temporary federal program that helped offset premium increases for Part D plans. The program began in 2025 as Medicare’s prescription drug benefit underwent major changes under the Inflation Reduction Act. Without it, enrollees would have seen their monthly premiums nearly double, according to a report from the Government Accountability Office.
The change will hurt seniors, Yaver said, noting that the program had reduced the average premium by 40% last year. People on Medicare are often retired and live on fixed incomes.
“Though seniors don’t change their Part D plans often, this year may be an exception, potentially resulting in seniors opting into lower-quality plans, leaving them less protected,” she said.
Enrollees will still have an annual out-of-pocket cap on prescription drugs. In 2027, the cap is $2,400.

title: North Korea looks abroad for talent in its scheme to infiltrate U.S. companies
summary: North Korea’s surreptitious push to plant employees in U.S. companies has expanded to include remote workers from other countries, such as Iran and Lebanon, according to U.S. government and foreign agencies and several cybersecurity researchers.
story: North Korea’s surreptitious push to plant employees in U.S. companies has expanded to include remote workers from other countries, such as Iran and Lebanon, according to U.S. government and foreign agencies and several cybersecurity researchers.

The scheme, estimated to involve thousands of workers applying to hundreds of American companies, generates hundreds of millions of dollars a year; the money is then laundered and used to fund the communist regime’s illicit weapons programs, according to U.S. government agencies.

U.S. authorities and companies have taken steps to counter the ruse, which has in turn pushed North Korea to get more creative. In July, the State Department and the Department of Justice put out a joint warning with several foreign agencies noting that North Korea is employing “increasingly sophisticated” tactics, including recruiting individuals outside its own country to help “obfuscate their identities and expand their activities globally.”

Government officials say North Korean teams are more frequently using people in foreign countries to participate as candidates in job interviews and sometimes establish in-person contact, in order to obtain work contracts. Once the job is secured, a North Korean agent typically takes over.

Iran is part of a growing list of countries including Syria, Lebanon, South Africa and Saudi Arabia, that have recently been cited by researchers as countries where North Korean teams are actively enlisting people to conduct on-camera interviews with Western companies. North Korea has long relied on U.S-based facilitators to receive and run company laptops and provide local internet access, but these internationally based individuals represent an expansion of the scheme’s accomplices.

According to a report from Flare, a cyber threat intelligence company, since 2024 at least 14 Iranians have been directly recruited by North Korean IT teams and at least two Iranians received formal offer letters from U.S. employers after successfully completing interview processes on behalf of applicants from North Korean IT teams. In one instance, a North Korean operator noted on internal tracking documents reviewed by Flare, that he’d contacted more than 50 Iranian engineers. It is not clear if operators accepted the roles offered to them.
Chris d’Eon, a threat intelligence researcher at Flare and contributor to the report, said Iranians make compelling targets for the North Korean scheme.

“From the North Korean operators’ perspective, this is a place where it is hard to get work internationally at a good price. It’s hard to do that sort of arbitrage with Western jobs and Western salaries,” he said.

Mirroring Western recruitment norms, foreign targets in some cases were identified on LinkedIn, given onboarding instructions and offer letters from North Korean teams, and later paid in cryptocurrency. In some instances, recruits were offered $500 a month to serve as part-time “interview associates” and coached to use false identities, according to Flare’s analysis of leaked North Korean communications.

“North Korea and Iran are very similar in that they’re sanctioned, and almost because of those sanctions, they have had to spend the last few decades developing their own science and technology education pipeline for their nuclear programs. So, there’s a lot of really highly educated STEM people in both North Korea and Iran for the exact same reason,” d’Eon said.

North Korea’s remote work schemes have proliferated since the pandemic, placing workers at U.S. companies in order to funnel money back to the regime and, in some cases, steal sensitive information. Those workers’ salaries are used in part to evade sanctions and fund the regime’s illicit programs, including its weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile efforts, according to U.S. government agencies. The United Nations estimates the schemes generate as much as $600 million annually, while the U.S. State Department-led sanctions monitoring assessment placed earnings for 2024 as high as $800 million.

In response, Western organizations’ HR and security teams have made efforts to equip hiring managers with tools to identify red flags and potential fraud. Candidates are sometimes prompted to wave their hand in front of their face to check for the use of AI filters or to say something negative about North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un. Using people from other countries to perform interviews is a way around those checks.

“It’s not a technical response to a problem; it’s now moving towards a physical response to a technical problem,” said Adrian Cheek, a senior cybercrime researcher at Flare who worked on Flare’s investigation.

Research by Kudelski Security, a cybersecurity firm, also found North Korean IT workers are now delegating parts of the interview process to developers elsewhere in the world who can pose as candidates and sometimes assist in passing technical tests.
In a 2026 investigation, Kudelski Security identified developers in Iran, Syria and South Africa who had accepted proposals from North Koreans after being approached on LinkedIn.

Beyond on-camera interview roles, North Korean teams are increasingly subcontracting their work, specifically targeting developers with the necessary skillsets, as they manage multiple jobs at once and look to scale the scheme.

Nigeria, Pakistan, India and parts of Latin America are also being targeted to assist in the scheme for facilitator recruitment, according to DTEX, a security company that tracks North Korea’s cybercrime.

In response to the joint government alert on the expansion of the IT scheme issued in July, North Korea’s Foreign Ministry released a statement rejecting the advisory, calling it a “nothing but a stereotyped political accusation with a sinister purpose to tarnish the image of our state.” A ministry spokesperson added, “The DPRK will never allow any politically and ideologically motivated attempt of the U.S. and other hostile forces to use the cyber issue as the means of criticism and pressure on other countries.”

North Korea doesn’t report economic data, but the Bank of Korea estimates North Korea’s real gross domestic product grew by 3.5% in 2025, marking the third consecutive year of growth over 3% in spite of global sanctions. Earnings from cyber crime are part of that growth, including IT work salaries and cryptocurrency heists, which net at least a billion each year, according to the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

“Because the costs are going up, the employers are trying to reduce the rate of growth, and the easiest way to reduce the rate of growth of healthcare costs is to push more of the costs onto the employee,” Schulman said.
Many appear prepared to do just that.
The Marsh survey found about two-thirds of large employers — those with 500 or more employees — said they expected to increase how much employees contribute toward their premiums in 2027.

Others may shift costs in other ways, including waiving copays and deductibles for primary care visits while charging for other kinds of care, or keeping premiums the same while raising the deductible.

For workers, that makes it important to look beyond the premium during open enrollment, Schulman said. A plan that costs less or about the same each paycheck may come with a higher deductible or require people to pay more when they seek care.
Medicare
Monthly premiums are handled somewhat differently for the roughly 70 million people enrolled in Medicare.

People on Medicare generally have more than one premium to consider: typically, a premium for Part B, which covers doctor’s visits and other outpatient care; and, for 9 out of 10 enrollees, a separate premium for Part D, which covers prescription drugs.
Prescription drug costs are where enrollees may see the biggest changes, according to Yaver, of the University of Pittsburgh.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projected in July that the baseline monthly cost for Part D coverage will rise about 6% in 2027, from $38.99 to $41.33.
What enrollees actually end up paying varies, depending on their income and their specific plan.

The increase stems from the Trump administration withdrawing its support for a temporary federal program that helped offset premium increases for Part D plans. The program began in 2025 as Medicare’s prescription drug benefit underwent major changes under the Inflation Reduction Act. Without it, enrollees would have seen their monthly premiums nearly double, according to a report from the Government Accountability Office.
The change will hurt seniors, Yaver said, noting that the program had reduced the average premium by 40% last year. People on Medicare are often retired and live on fixed incomes.
“Though seniors don’t change their Part D plans often, this year may be an exception, potentially resulting in seniors opting into lower-quality plans, leaving them less protected,” she said.
Enrollees will still have an annual out-of-pocket cap on prescription drugs. In 2027, the cap is $2,400.

title: Saudi shutdown of key pipeline limits oil flow as Yemen hits back against Houthis
summary: Saudi Arabia has closed a critical oil pipeline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq, the latest squeeze on Middle Eastern supplies after attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels this week threatened to deepen the world’s energy crisis.
story: Saudi Arabia has closed a critical oil pipeline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq, the latest squeeze on Middle Eastern supplies after attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels this week threatened to deepen the world’s energy crisis.

The 745-mile pipeline had helped Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest crude oil exporter, bypass the blocked Strait of Hormuz, through which some 20% of the world’s oil used to pass before the U.S. and Israel waged war on Iran in late February.

The Saudi Energy Ministry confirmed the shutdown of the East-West pipeline on Friday, adding that drone attacks had resulted in a number of injuries and that its teams were “taking the necessary measures to secure the pipeline and assess its safety.”

Saudi Arabia said it would not retaliate for now following a request from Iraq’s prime minister, while reserving the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security and critical facilities, according to a Saudi foreign ministry statement.
The pipeline has been moving 4-5% of global oil supplies, new agency Reuters reported Friday.

An Iraqi military commander was dismissed early on Saturday after investigations confirmed the latest drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia originated from Iraq, according to a statement by Iraq‘s prime minister’s office.
Iraq also closed two key border crossings with Iran, Iraq’s state-run news agency reported Saturday.

Kuwait, a U.S. ally in the region, warned that the pipeline attack was a “dangerous escalation that undermines the security and stability of the region,” while Bahrain stressed Saudi Arabia’s right to “take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty.”

U.S. President Donald Trump said on ⁠Saturday that everything would “work out just ⁠fine” when asked about the region on a visit to Ireland. He also said, without providing evidence, that Iran was “probably” behind the pipeline attack.

The pipeline strikes came as rebel Houthi forces in Yemen captured Perim, an island in the middle of the vital Bab el Mandeb Strait, which serves as a gateway to the Red Sea trade route that links Europe and Asia.

The Houthis also captured the historic port city of Mocha this week, followed by an advance on the strategic coastal town of Dhubab and the apparent withdrawal of forces from the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government from Perim, also known as Mayun.

If the Houthis are able to threaten shipping along the Bab el Mandeb Strait, it could reduce oil supplies through another key waterway. Saudi Arabia has had to rely on the Red Sea route given the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz.
Yemeni Ministry of Defense said Saturday it had carried out counterattacks against Houthi targets, hitting militants, vehicles and weaponry.

A statement issued by Houthi forces on Friday said that “maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels,” vowing to strike Saudi targets “until the aggression stops and the blockade against our dear people is lifted.”
Trump said the Houthis had contacted the U.S. to stress that they “don’t want to fight with us” and would “much prefer not having us involved.”
Oil prices ended the week above $100 a barrel for the first time since Mid-May after the dramatic developments.

Effective Houthi control over the Red Sea coast “is a game changer,” and could give Iran powerful new leverage in its war with the United States, Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics, told NBC News.
He said: “Far from being really besieged and bleeding, Iran now could easily increase the pain to the U.S. economy and the world economy.”
Gerges said it remains to be seen whether the Houthis can maintain their control of the vast areas of the Red Coast, or if they “overextended themselves.”

But the Trump administration “now finds itself in a much more difficult position because it gambled that the blockade of Iran would force Iran to accept Trump’s conditions,” he added. “The reverse has happened.”

Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian said Saturday that it would sign an agreement with Oman over a joint route through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, as part of a deal securing future navigation rights through the strait.
That deal is not expected to immediately reopen the waterway without a broader agreement with the U.S., Iran has previously stressed.

The U.S. military is helping its Saudi counterparts to develop and coordinate targets inside Yemen, according to a U.S. official and a person familiar with the matter, after Saudi Arabia vowed a firm response to hostilities.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman is urging President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, according to a person familiar with the matter. The president and the Crown Prince have discussed the recent escalation by the Houthis at least twice in the last 24 hours, this person said Friday.
The United Nations’ International Organization for Migration warned on Friday at least 46,000 people have so far been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week.
It said that figure spanned the West Coast and Taiz governorates as of Thursday, with the numbers of those displaced “alarmingly rising by the hour.”
The organization called on all parties to the conflict to “guarantee safe humanitarian access and to protect civilians, aid workers and assets on the ground.”

title: Board votes to rename Nashville International Airport for Dolly Parton
summary: Nashville’s airport authority board unanimously voted Friday to begin the process to rename the city’s airport to honor late country music legend and Tennessee icon Dolly Parton.
story: Nashville’s airport authority board unanimously voted Friday to begin the process to rename the city’s airport to honor late country music legend and Tennessee icon Dolly Parton.
The vote by the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority did not establish a new name for Nashville International Airport, but it begins the process, the board said in a statement.
“It’s official!” Nashville International Airport said on social media when announcing the 6-0 airport authority vote, which the board described as “the first step in a multifaceted process.”
Parton, beloved by country music fans around the world, died last month at the age of 80 after a brief battle with cancer, her family said on Aug. 25.
Nashville board votes to rename airport for Dolly Parton

“While a final name has not yet been determined, we are working closely with the appropriate parties to thoughtfully determine how Dolly Parton’s name and legacy will be incorporated,” the airport authority said.
The airport authority said that it anticipates having more definitive plans to share about the implementation in the coming months.
“We are grateful for the tremendous support and enthusiasm from our community and Dolly’s fans around the world,” it said. “We look forward to sharing additional details as plans are finalized.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee thanked the airport authority board for its action Friday and called the vote an “important step to honor her remarkable legacy.”
“Dolly has always helped the world fall in love with Tennessee,” he said.

title: Man arrested in connection with death of Tasia Fortune in Mississippi
summary: A man has been arrested in the death of Tasia Fortune, the 29-year-old Black woman who was found hanging from a tree in Mississippi last month, police announced Friday.
story: A man has been arrested in the death of Tasia Fortune, the 29-year-old Black woman who was found hanging from a tree in Mississippi last month, police announced Friday.

Jarques Ratliff was arrested Friday afternoon and will be charged with homicide, Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney told reporters. She said he had an “association” with Fortune, but did not disclose what kind.

Fortune’s body was discovered Aug. 3 behind an abandoned building in Jackson. Her family had previously said they did not believe Fortune died by suicide. The case sparked widespread alarm and media attention given Mississippi’s sordid history with racial violence.
Her death was officially classified as a homicide Thursday evening, Brackney said. That determination led police to secure two search warrants and an arrest warrant for Ratliff, she said.

Investigators served the search warrants Friday, but Ratliff was not found at the location. Officers heading back to headquarters later found him walking along Capitol Street and took him into custody, Brackney said.

“The arrest today is an important development in this investigation, but it is not the conclusion. This case remains active, and additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence wherever it leads,” she said, adding: “because Tasia and her children deserve nothing less.”
It’s not immediately clear whether Ratliff has retained an attorney.
Brackney said the Fortune family was immediately notified of the arrest.
Christy Spivey, Fortune’s mother, told The Associated Press that after she learned of the arrest, she “just started crying and told them ‘thank you, thank you, thank you.’”
Spivey, who did not know Ratliff, said the family is “in disbelief” and that they “still don’t have a lot of answers.” Police did not share a motive or whether DNA led to the arrest, she told the AP.
While Fortune’s death has been ruled a homicide, Brackney — who was cautious as she described Fortune as found “in a hanging position” — did not elaborate on the cause of death determination.

The chief acknowledged the scrutiny into the case, saying, “We understand the questions and the desire for answers given Mississippi’s history,” but stressed the case must be based on evidence and facts.

title: Democrats shift their mail voting message: From the Politics Desk
summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Jane C. Timm and Natasha Korecki explore how Democrats are pushing early and in-person voting amid mail ballot concerns. Plus, Kristen Welker examines whether the GOP’s midterm convention can help the party solve a key dilemma this fall.
— Adam Wollner
Democrats shift their mail voting message

Democrats and progressive groups are urging voters to cast their ballots as early as possible — and increasingly, in person — amid concerns that President Donald Trump’s intervention and postal delays could disrupt the mail voting process this fall.

Less than eight weeks from Election Day, the legal fate of an executive order from Trump that would restrict mail voting remains unclear, with a ruling from the Supreme Court over whether it can be implemented expected soon. Aside from the order, budget issues and operational changes to the U.S. Postal Service have slowed mail delivery.
Since the Covid pandemic, Democrats in particular have championed mail voting, which their voters have relied on more than Republicans’ in recent elections.
But ahead of the midterms, with control of the House and Senate up for grabs, they have pumped the brakes on that message.

“State parties traditionally really pushed two key messages when it came to voting: Vote on Election Day or vote by mail. And when we talked about voting by mail, it was, ‘Get your ballot back by Election Day,’” said Jane Kleeb, who chairs the Association of State Democratic Committees and serves as a Democratic National Committee vice chair. “This time around, we are really pushing people … to say, ‘Vote early in person. Go to your county election office and vote early in person.’ And that this is the best way that we can get Democrats elected is if you vote early in person.”

While Democrats are putting a greater emphasis on in-person voting this year, they aren’t discouraging voters if they want to cast a ballot by mail. Rather, Kleeb said the party will stress that they need to put their ballots in the mail or a drop box well before Election Day.
“We say that we still believe that voting by mail is safe and secure,” she said. “This election cycle in particular, you need to give an extra week for your ballot to arrive in time.”
Read more →
Can the midterm convention rally Trump’s base?

With their midterm convention in Dallas this week, Republicans attempted to confront one of their biggest dilemmas heading into November: how to fire up President Donald Trump’s loyal base when he’s not on the ballot.

“Pretend that I’m on the ballot,” Trump told the crowd Wednesday night. On Thursday night, Trump had attendees raise their hands and “pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States” that “on Nov. 3 we are going to go out and vote.”

As part of his pitch, Trump said that the government would pay each adult American a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans maintained control of the House and Senate, though there are major questions around how such a plan would work.

Trump and other Republican speakers at the convention also cast Democrats as extreme and out of touch, often labeling them communists. It does raise the question of whether Republicans are failing to appreciate the energy on the left, which has fueled progressive victories and sky-high turnout in primaries this year.
Turning out the president’s supporters could be key to holding on to the Senate, given that states like Texas, Iowa, Alaska and Ohio that Trump won by double digits in 2024 could decide the majority.

But Republicans will also need to appeal to independents and moderate voters in crucial swing states like Michigan and North Carolina. And the GOP still faces significant headwinds heading into November, even among Trump’s most ardent supporters.

While Republicans still broadly support the president, the share who “strongly approve” of his job performance has dropped 11 points since the spring to 41%, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey. Trump’s overall job approval among Americans is at 36%.
That’s in line with a new Quinnipiac University poll of registered voters that showed Trump’s job approval at 33% and Democrats with an 11-point lead in the battle for Congress.
The GOP’s struggles come amid widespread opposition to the Iran war and concerns about the cost of living, particularly high gas prices, including among Republicans.

Vice President JD Vance acknowledged those concerns during his convention speech Thursday, imploring supporters, “Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater.” He added, “Don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.”

Trump also acknowledged this week for the first time that he does not expect the Iran war to end or for gas prices to come down before the midterms. So while the president may have fired up his supporters in Dallas, the bigger test will come when voters head to the polls in 53 days.

We’ll discuss the fight ahead in the midterms on “Meet the Press” this Sunday with Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. I’ll also speak with Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic researcher who sounded the alarm about the threats from artificial intelligence.

🎈More from the convention: Republicans attempted to address voters’ economic concerns, with speakers mentioning themes of affordability, prices and costs at least 178 times, according to an analysis by NBC News. On the other hand, the Iran war was largely ignored.

Read more →🔵 Shifting sands: In at least five battleground races, Democratic candidates have declared their opposition to transgender athletes competing in women’s and girls sports, a pivot from their party’s long-standing position. Read more →🗳️ We have a winner: The Indiana Supreme Court ruled after a monthslong recount that a Republican state senator narrowly defeated his Trump-backed challenger in the May primary. There is also a growing debate in Washington about whether the Office of the Director of National Intelligence has fulfilled its intended goals and whether it should be drastically reformed or even scrapped altogether.

title: Florida DMV says it was hacked shortly after major driver’s license breach
summary: Florida’s Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles said Friday that it’s investigating a data breach, making it the second organization that hosts Americans’ driver’s license information to be hacked this month.
story: Florida’s Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles (FLHSMV) said Friday that it’s investigating a data breach, making it the second organization that hosts Americans’ driver’s license information to be hacked this month.

The Florida announcement comes on the heels of another incident, in which a vendor that scans Americans’ driver’s licenses for private companies, IDscan.net, said it was investigating a major data breach of its own. Hackers claimed to have stolen 160 million IDs from the company, including one from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, sparking federal investigations.

While the two hacks do not appear to be related, they highlight how cybercriminals, whose jobs keep getting easier thanks to AI, can easily gain access to millions of Americans’ extremely sensitive personal information.

Specifics of what was stolen from the FLHSMV are scant. But the department said in a statement published to its website that the breach was “conducted by an international cybercriminal organization.” Law enforcement is investigating the hack, the agency said, and the breach has since been contained. It’s unclear how long the hackers had access.

Last week, ShinyHunters, a cybercriminal group that hacks targets for sensitive information and then extorts them for a payment to delete it, announced on its dark-web site that the “Florida DMV” was its latest victim.

That website, viewed by NBC News, gave a deadline of Sept. 11 for Florida to negotiate a fee not to release hacked files. It included a single sample file, a screengrab of an image allegedly from Florida’s Driver and Vehicle Information Database, that showed the alleged driver’s license for late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, a former Florida resident. NBC News was unable to verify the authenticity of the image, which includes Epstein’s alleged Social Security number, former driver’s license number and vehicles registered in his name.

On Friday afternoon, after the FLHSMV published its statement, ShinyHunters deleted references to Florida. It’s not clear why the posting was deleted in this instance, but Ian Gray, vice president of intelligence at the threat monitoring company Flashpoint, said that is often an indication that the state had reached out to the hackers to discuss a potential payment not to leak hacked information.
“When a victim is missing from a blog, it typically means that there was a negotiation,” he said.
The FLHSMV did not respond to questions on whether it was engaging with ShinyHunters.

On Sept. 3, independent journalist Brian Krebs published an investigation that found a hacker group claimed to have hacked a driver’s license scanning company and was selling access to a tool that could access millions of Americans’ licenses.

The company, IDscan.net, did not respond to requests for comment, but said on its website the next day that “an unauthorized third party may have accessed and/or copied certain customer information stored within their accounts on the IDScan.net cloud.”
An FBI spokesperson confirmed to NBC News that the agency is investigating that breach.

title: ‘The Carol Burnett Show’ Turns 59. Carol Burnett and Tim Conway Reflect on Their Hilarious Antics in 1995 TODAY Interview
summary: Carol Burnett and Tim Conway stopped by TODAY in 1995 to reminisce about “The Carol Burnett Show.”
story: Welcome to the “TODAY Archives,” where we revisit memories from our show when celebrities and newsmakers started discourse, made us laugh or shaped our culture. This latest installment highlights “The Carol Burnett Show” and a visit to TODAY from the show’s star and Tim Conway, who reminisced about their classic comedy series on March 3, 1995 .
Nearly six decades after it premiered, “The Carol Burnett Show” still has fans laughing.

The CBS series premiered Sept. 11, 1967, and ran for 11 seasons before concluding its run in 1978. Along with co-stars Tim Conway, Harvey Korman, Vicki Lawrence and Lyle Waggoner, Carol Burnett kept fans in stitches with uproarious skits and parodies.
The show won 25 Emmy Awards and was nominated for 45 more, cementing its place in TV lore.

On March 3, 1995, Burnett and Conway, who died in 2019 at the age of 85, visited TODAY to reminisce about the series with Katie Couric, which gave Burnett the chance to open up about Conway’s flair for making his castmates laugh.
“When Conway was on, he was relentless. He would do things that we never expected, and nobody knew what was going to happen,” she said.
The Cast Had Tons of Fun
Conway felt the cast truly enjoyed themselves making the show, while also praising Burnett.
“I would say that we probably had the best time of a lot of people on television,” he said.

“This lady, not only is she the nicest lady probably you’ll ever meet — it’s so annoying because she never says anything about anybody — and just surrounded herself with those kinds of people,” Conway said. “And it was just a place you wanted to be.”
Who Was Carol Burnett’s Favorite Character?
Burnett played a lot of characters on the show, but when asked who her favorite is, she had no doubt.
“I think it was Eunice,” she said.
Her portrayal of the melodramatic Eunice holds a special place in her heart.

“She started out as such a witch. She was just horrible,” she said. “And then as it developed, you could understand where her rage was coming from. It was this mother feeling trapped, and her dreams of being a movie star, of course, were ridiculous. But she always wanted to be better than what she was.”
What About That Classic ‘Went with the Wind!’ Sketch?

This Season 10 spoof of “Gone with the Wind” featured Burnett as Starlett O’Hara, who wears a dress made out of her window curtain, with the rod going across her back. It’s a classic sketch and one that Burnett said scored more laughs than it may have originally.

“(Costume designer) Bob Mackie said, ‘I have an idea.’ I said, ‘What?’ And he came out with the curtain rod and the dress on it, and I fell on the floor,” she recalled. “I said, ‘This is absolute genius.’”

title: Reverend Shares Lessons From His Mom Who Died in 9/11 After Going Back to Get Her Purse
summary: Elizabeth Holmes, one of thousands who lost their lives on Sept.
story: Elizabeth Holmes, one of thousands who lost their lives on Sept. 11, 2001, originally made it out from the 84th floor of the south tower that day. But after reaching the staircase with her friend and realizing she had forgotten her purse, Holmes ran back inside.
Her son, Reverend Miles Travis Boyd Jr., was just 12 years old when he lost his mother in the terrorist attacks.

On the 25th anniversary of the national tragedy, Boyd, now the senior pastor at Sharon Baptist Church in the Bronx, sat down with TODAY to reflect on his memory of Holmes, what her decision to retrieve her belongings represents and how he is carrying on her legacy.

Boyd, who released a book about the experience ahead of the anniversary, “The Purse She Left Behind: A Son’s Memory, A Mother’s Legacy,” explained why he explored his grief, faith and purpose through his mother’s accessory.

“When I think of this, I think of my mom and what that meant culturally for women, right, you don’t leave your purse just anywhere, your livelihood is in your purse,” Boyd said of the book’s title. “So I decided what way to better tell her legacy by speaking of the truth that she was impacted by at that moment.”

Boyd told TODAY hosts Dylan Dreyer, Craig Melvin and Al Roker that at the time of the attacks, he was sleeping at his aunt’s house in Manhattan. That morning, Boyd said, his uncle woke him up told him to turn on the news and to call his mother.

“I immediately called, and to no avail, I got no message or any pickup,” Boyd explained. “I called her boss, and I called her supervisor, because I was the kid who had everyone’s number. All the lines were busy at that point. My uncle took me and my cousin onto the roof just to see what would happen.”

While he wasn’t able to reach his mom, Boyd recalled that he still believed that she would come home — especially since she had already survived the World Trade Center bombing in 1993 that killed six and injured thousands more.

Over the next few years, Holmes was never found, but Boyd said he still held out hope that she would turn up and walk down the aisle at church years later. It wasn’t until he went off to college that Boyd came to terms with the loss.

“My first day in college, I am putting up pictures on the wall, and there was this one little picture of my mother and I left, this perfect square of the picture, and that’s when I realized that Mom wasn’t coming home,” Boyd said.

Since the attacks, Boyd says he’s also been remembering his mother beyond the loss, reflecting on her lessons from having a strong faith, to the importance of education and leading a life dedicated to making a difference.
For 14 years, Boyd taught kids in his hometown in Harlem before pursuing ministry full time.

Rev. Al Sharpton, a Baptist minister, civil rights and social justice activist and radio-television personality, took in the then-12-year-old after the tragedy to provide a sense of normalcy and support when Boyd’s family was searching the city for his mother.
Al Sharpton surprised Boyd on TODAY with a video message, commemorating his dedication to his mother’s legacy.

“Travis, I’m so proud of you,” Sharpton said in the video. “I remember 25 years ago how you stayed with us. Every time the phone rang, hoping it was that your mother was calling. She never called, but you never let her down. I’m so proud of you, and I know she is.”
Boyd’s book, “The Purse She Left Behind: A Son’s Memory, A Mother’s Legacy,” is out now.

title: Four Former Presidents Reunite in Downtown NYC to Attend 9/11 Memorial Ceremony
summary: Former presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, George W. Bush and Joe Biden were present at the somber ceremony at the National Sept. 11 Memorial in downtown Manhattan. They were also joined by former first ladies, Hillary Clinton, Michelle Obama, Laura Bush and Jill Biden.
story: As the nation marks the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, four former U.S. presidents attended New York City’s commemorative ceremony.

Former presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, George W. Bush and Joe Biden were present at the somber ceremony at the National Sept. 11 Memorial in downtown Manhattan. They were also joined by former first ladies, Hillary Clinton, Michelle Obama, Laura Bush and Jill Biden.
Several other officials and politicians, including Vice President JD Vance and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, were also in attendance.
President Donald Trump remained in Washington, D.C. to attend a ceremony at the Pentagon.
At the memorial, the former presidents stood up solemnly as a youth choir sang the national anthem.
Though none of the four made public remarks at the ceremony, some of the former presidents recently shared their thoughts and reflections on the tragedy.
In a statement posted on social media, Bill Clinton said that “we can’t erase the nightmare that so many have lived through and are still living with today.”

“But we can support the people who have given and lost so much by treating one another with respect, in person and online, and recognizing that what we have in common is far more important than what divides us,” Clinton said in the statement shared on X.

Clinton partnered with the late Sen. Bob Dole, his Republican opponent in the 1996 general election, to launch the Families of Freedom Scholarship Fund shortly after the attacks. He said in his statement that the fund has awarded more than $193 million in scholarships to nearly 4,000 children and spouses of people who were killed or permanently disabled by the attacks.
Former President Barack Obama and first lady Michelle Obama shared a statement on social media in remembrance of Sept. 11, 2001.

In the statement, the Obamas said that they are “remembering those we lost that day and those who made the ultimate sacrifice in the wars that followed.” They also said that they are praying for the families who lost loved ones that day.
“We hope Americans everywhere remember the true lesson of 9/11: that we can survive even our darkest days as long as we move forward as one nation and one people,” the Obamas said in the statement.
On Sept. 9 at the George W. Bush Presidential Center in Dallas, Former President George W. Bush recalled his first message to the nation following the terrorist attacks in 2001.
Bush was visiting schoolchildren in Florida when he was told by an aide that a second plane had hit the World Trade Center in Manhattan.

“I didn’t have much time to process that, but it was pretty clear to me that if we were under attack, then my job was to defend the child that was reading to me, and her family, and her country,” Bush said, according to a broadcast of the event by C-SPAN.
“In this case, I became a wartime president,” he added.

title: When Are the Emmys? How to Watch 2026 Awards Show
summary: The 78th Emmy Awards will see some of the biggest Hollywood stars going head to head in the major categories.
story: The 78th Emmy Awards will see some of the biggest Hollywood stars going head to head in the major categories.

The 2026 Emmy Awards, television’s biggest night, will be held on Monday, Sept. 14, in Los Angeles. The ceremony will be broadcast live from Peacock Theater and feature nominees like Zendaya, Oscar Isaac, Steve Carell, Colman Domingo and more.
Nominations were first revealed on July 8, with TODAY exclusively sharing the nominees for outstanding variety series and outstanding reality competition program.

After all the categories were announced, “The Pitt” led with a staggering 25 nominations. “Hacks” closely followed with 24 nods for its fifth and final season, which set a record in the comedy category. Rounding out the top three was new series “Widow’s Bay” with 19 nominations.
There were also 28 actors who received their first-ever Emmy nominations.
Some of them have already added “Emmy winner” to their resume, as last week awards were handed out at the Creative Arts Emmys. Soon more stars will be presented with the coveted golden statue.
Read on to learn everything you need to know about the 2026 Emmys.
When Are the 2026 Emmys?
The 2026 Emmys are set to air live on Monday, Sept. 14, beginning at 5 p.m. PT/ 8 p.m. ET.
The ceremony will be held at Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.
How to Watch and Stream the 2026 Emmys
The show will be broadcast from coast-to-coast on NBC and will stream live and on demand on Peacock, as well.
Nights one and two from the Creative Arts Emmys will air on FXX on Saturday, Sept. 12, at 8 p.m. ET/PT. It will be available to stream on Hulu the following day.
Who Is Hosting the 2026 Emmys?
The Television Academy announced in July that Mariska Hargitay will emcee the event.

Hargitay also scored two nominations for her film “My Mom Jayne,” and won for outstanding documentary and outstanding directing for a documentary/nonfiction program, making her a three-time Emmy winner.
This will be the first time a woman is leading the ceremony since Jane Lynch hosted in 2011.
Speaking about the honor during an appearance on TODAY in August, Hargitay shared that it took her a minute to process that she was being asked to host the major award show.
“I thought about it over the weekend and then I started going, ‘Why not?’” she recalled.

“Which is where I kind of am in my life,” the “Law & Order: SVU” star continued. “I was so incredibly honored and, again, knowing that it’s the first woman in 15 years was absolutely thrilling. And I am somebody to take on new challenges.”
Who Is Presenting at the 2026 Emmys?
Leading up to the ceremony, the Television Academy has been sharing groups of celebrities who will be presenters.
