title: 9/11 Movies and Documentaries Worth Watching
summary: In the 25 years since September 11, 2001, filmmakers and documentarians have been trying to capture the events of that tragic day in a number of ways.
story: This year marks 25 years since Sept. 11, 2001, a day many Americans will never forget.

Some will recall the moment they learned or watched in a news report that two planes downed the twin towers of New York City’s World Trade Center. The devastation continued as a third plane struck the Pentagon outside Washington, D.C. Then, there was a failed attempt by a fourth plane, which crashed in rural Pennsylvania when the passengers took over.
These horrific and fatal events are etched in the memories of U.S. citizens and others around the world.

In the ensuing decades, filmmakers have released numerous 9/11 documentaries and fictionalized depictions that explore the events before, during and after. As Sept. 11, 2026 marks the 25th anniversary of those attacks, TODAY has compiled a list of 17 films  for those wanting to look back in remembrance or educate young people who may not have been alive during the historic moment.
1. “The Man Who Knew” (2002)
Watch on YouTube. (1 hour, 25 mins.)

PBS’ “Frontline” has been on top of numerous documentaries about 9/11 and its aftermath; “The Man Who Knew” focuses on a former FBI counterterrorism agent who felt the U.S. should have preemptively taken out Osama Bin Laden. John O’Neill, who died in the twin towers on 9/11, had been fighting for six years to track down and prosecute al-Qaeda operatives around the world, but was considered controversial.
2. “Fahrenheit 9/11” (2004)
Watch on Tubi, Pluto TV or The Roku Channel. (2 hours, 3 mins.)

Director Michael Moore put himself behind and in front of the camera to cast his unflinching gaze on the presidency of George W. Bush, the Iraq War and the way the media covered the war, along with how the administration dealt with the events of 9/11.
3. “Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close” (2011)
Watch on YouTube. (2 hours, 9 mins.)

“Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close” stars Tom Hanks and Sandra Bullock and is based on a bestselling fiction book by Jonathan Safran Foer. It follows a young boy named Oskar as he goes on a quest across New York with a key, one year after his father died in the World Trade Center attacks.
4. “The Woman Who Wasn’t There” (2012)
Watch on YouTube, Pluto TV or Fandango. (1 hour, 4 mins.)

Based on the story of Alicia Esteve Head, “The Woman Who Wasn’t There” was both a book and a documentary that looked at a Spanish businesswoman who claimed to have survived the World Trade Center attacks (calling herself Tania Head). She became the head of the World Trade Center Survivors’ Network support group — but in 2007, her story was revealed to be a hoax.
5. “9/11 Inside the Pentagon” (2016)
Watch on PBS Passport. (54 mins.)

The twin towers weren’t the only buildings hit on 9/11; the Pentagon was struck by a third plane, and 184 people were killed. This documentary shifts the perspective from New York to one of the country’s most important and secretive buildings to explore the attack.
6. “In the Shadow of the Towers: Stuyvesant High on 9/11” (2019)
Watch on HBO Max, YouTube, Hulu or Prime Video. (32 mins.)

Students in one of New York City’s most elite schools, Stuyvesant High, watched the World Trade Center attack from their classrooms. Director Amy Schatz spoke with former students who shared their recollections. (TODAY.com also has a story told through the eyes of adults who were in kindergarten blocks away from the twin towers at the time.)
Watch on Peacock, YouTube or The Roku Channel. (1 hour, 45 mins.)

The U.S. Capitol and White House were spared being hit by a fourth plane on 9/11 when passengers wrestled control from the terrorists inside. That plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. All 44 inside, including the hijackers, were killed. “United 93” is a fictionalized re-telling of these events, directed by Paul Greengrass.
8. “9/11: The Final Minutes of Flight 93” (2020)
Watch on YouTube, Tubi or The History Channel. (43 mins.)

While “United 93” is a scripted feature film looking at the plane crash in Pennsylvania, “9/11: The Final Minutes of Flight 93” is a documentary. It provides newly unclassified evidence that allowed filmmakers to piece together what happened on the plane, minute by minute.
9. “The Forever Prisoner” (2021)
Watch or HBO Max. (2 hours)

Oscar winner Alex Gibney co-executive produced the 10-part fictionalized take on the events leading up to 9/11 with an adaptation of the 2006 book “The Looming Tower” in 2018. In “The Forever Prisoner,” he dives into the aftermath of al-Qaeda suspect Abu Zubaydah, the first high-value detainee who was subjected to “enhanced interrogation techniques” for the U.S. post-9/11.
10. “9/11: Inside the President’s War Room” (2021)
Watch on Apple TV or Prime Video. (1 hour, 30 mins.)

This Apple TV+/BBC One documentary goes into detail about the steps that followed in the immediate hours after the 9/11 attacks, focused on the point of view of President George W. Bush and his staff. It includes interviews with Bush, former Vice President Dick Cheney, Condoleezza Rice, Colin Powell and many others.
11. “9/11: One Day in America” (2021)
Watch on Hulu and Disney+. (6 episodes, run times vary)

In its six episodes, “One Day in America” (which was created in official collaboration with the 9/11 Memorial & Museum) walks viewers through the timeline of 9/11 while focusing on those who survived and those who came to their rescue: firefighters, paramedics and regular folk.
12. “Turning Point: 9/11 and the War on Terror” (2021)
Watch on Netflix. (5 episodes, run times vary.)
In this five-episode series, experts explore where the 9/11 attacks came from, what happened the day-of and the decadeslong ripple effect the attack has had on the U.S. and its citizens.
13. “Zero Dark Thirty” (2012)
Watch on Netflix, The Roku Channel, Prime Video or Apple TV. (2 hours, 37 mins)

This drama directed by Kathryn Bigelow follows the efforts to find al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden after the 9/11 attacks. The film, which stars Jessica Chastain, Chris Pratt, Kyle Chandler and Joel Edgerton, was nominated for five Academy Awards, including best picture, and won one for sound editing.
14. “Twin Towers: Legacy” (2025)
Watch on Tubi, PlutoTV, The Roku Channel or Fandango. (1 hour, 27 mins)

This film narrated by Dennis Quaid is a follow-up to 2003’s “Twin Towers,” an Oscar-winning documentary about the actions taken by policeman Joe Vigiano during the 9/11 attacks. “Twin Towers: Legacy” follows Vigiano’s sons as they try to honor their father who died that day.
15. “102 Minutes That Changed America” (2008)
Watch on Tubi, PlutoTV or The History Channel. (1 hour, 42 min)

This documentary originally aired on History and won three Emmy Awards. Featuring amateur video and voicemails, it captures the events of 9/11 in New York City between the time the first World Trade Center was attacked and the fall of the second tower.
16. “Top of the World” (2026)
Watch on CNN streaming service. (40 mins.)

This documentary is being released as the 25th anniversary of 9/11 arrives. It also coincides with the 50th anniversary of the opening of Windows on the World, the restaurant that sat atop the World Trade Center. This film includes firsthand accounts from former staff members, sharing how the community was impacted after the attack killed all 79 employees working that morning and their 91 guests.
17. “Turning Point: Generation 9/11” (2026)
Watch on Netflix. (1 hour, 39 mins.)

Twenty-five years after the attack, multiple generations, from survivors, to children who lost parents, journalists, Afghans and U.S. Marines, share how their lives were affected. They also reflect on how they process their grief today.

title: Dolly Parton’s First Posthumous Song, ‘Bound to Ride,’ Features Her Beloved Sense of Humor
summary: Two weeks after her death, Dolly Parton’s fans are getting to hear the icon’s first song released posthumously.
story: Two weeks after her death, Dolly Parton’s fans are getting to hear the icon’s first song released posthumously.

The country music legend and actor died following “a brief battle with cancer” her estate announced Aug. 25. She was 80. As the news was reported, tributes poured in from her peers and fans. They reflected on Parton’s impact in the industry, from hits like “9 to 5” to “I Will Always Love You” and “Jolene.”

Now, they’ll have the opportunity to listen to a new song from her once more, as Parton is featured on an upcoming all-star tribute album titled “Where the Soul Never Dies: Celebrating 80 Years of The Stanley Brothers.”
She added her vocals to the track “Bound to Ride,” which the country duo recorded in 1964, and the single has been posted on YouTube ahead of the album’s release on Oct. 16.

Parton originally recorded her part around 2022 in her personal studio, Rolling Stone reports. The album is also set to include vocals by Willie Nelson and Sierra Ferrell, Dierks Bentley with Della Mae, and Steve Martin and Ed Helms, among others.
Following Parton’s death, her longtime manager Danny Nozell shared a lengthy list of all the projects that the country superstar had been working on and was excited to bring to life.

“Dolly worked up until the day she died. She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy,” Nozell said in a press release. “Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come.”
Among Parton’s future plans are Dolly Dolls, Dolly’s Cup Of Ambition Coffee, Dolly’s Dog Treats and her Broadway musical, among many others.
Her manager stressed that anything that is released on the singer’s official channels, Parton “placed her personal stamp on it.”
He added that they will continue to share more details on additional projects, including an avatar show, a biopic, docuseries, scripted series and a Billy The Kid animated series, “soon.”
For now, fans can enjoy listening once more to Parton and her beloved voice and sense of humor.

title: Alison Brie Goes Blonde and Confirms a New Role: ‘It’s For a Part!’
summary: Alison Brie just underwent a stylish and lighter hairstyle. The actor, known for her brunette locks, is now a blonde.
story: Alison Brie is back to blonde.
The former “Community” star debuted her new hair color at the 2026 Daytime Beauty Awards red carpet in Los Angeles on Sept. 9.
“They *do* have more fun?!” Brie said on her Instagram story, commenting on her new look.
As someone complimented her blondest ‘do to date, Brie revealed the reason for it.
“It’s for a part!” Brie said in a TikTok shared by “Entertainment Tonight.”
Just three days prior, Brie showcased her typical brunette look at the Creative Arts Emmys, where she supported her “GLOW” co-star Betty Gilpin and her win for “Widow’s Bay.”
This is not the first time she’s sported lighter locks. In 2019, Brie teased a new role with a transformation reveal on Instagram.
“When your husband asks you to ‘go blonde’ for a role... you say yes😉,” she wrote in the caption.
That “role” turned out to be the 2020 horror thriller “The Rental.”
Now, blonder than ever, and with a few inches off, fans are wondering what role called for the change.
Brie has recently starred in “Masters Of The Universe” and “Together.”

Brie is confirmed to appear in Peacock’s “Community: The Movie,” which has experienced ongoing production delays. In the original sitcom, however, which ran from 2009 to 2015, Brie’s character Annie Edison was a brunette.
Brie is also in cahoots with Alice Stanley Jr. for a female-driven horror comedy, but is said to be making her directorial feature debut rather than any on-camera work.

title: Cindy Crawford Describes Meeting Son of Ex-Husband Richard Gere
summary: Nearly 40 years after Cindy Crawford and Richard Gere stepped out as one of the iconic couples of the early 1990s, their children are now starring together on the FX show “The Shards.”
story: Nearly 40 years after Cindy Crawford and Richard Gere stepped out as one of the iconic couples of the early 1990s, their children are now starring together on the FX show “The Shards.”

Homer Gere, 26, and Kaia Gerber, 25, are part of the cast of the teen serial killer drama helmed by Ryan Murphy and posed together on the cover of the September issue of Vogue. Their parents posed together for Vogue in 1992, making the latest cover shot a full-circle moment between the children of the supermodel and the actor, who divorced in 1995 after four years of marriage.

Crawford, 60, shared on TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle Sept. 10 what it’s like to see the two working together and how she first met Homer Gere, who is Richard Gere’s son with actor Carey Lowell. Gerber is the daughter of Crawford and her husband Rande Gerber.
“I had never met Homer,” Crawford said. “I met him while they were filming. He’s lovely, and Kaia enjoyed working with him.”
Crawford also expanded on how the two young actors deal with being labeled “nepo babies.”

“They’re both in the same situation,” Crawford said. “They understand it’s going to be a question they’re going to get asked, but at the same time they both work really hard and think they’re both doing a great job.”
Crawford emphasized that Gerber works hard for her modeling and acting career.
“Look, there’s pros and cons to having famous parents,” Crawford added. “And I know sometimes it feels like pressure, or she feels like, ‘Wow.’”
For example, her daughter can do a modeling shoot and commenters may bring up that her mother wore the look first.

“I’m like, ‘I know,’ because I can talk about my mom and no one knew who that was, and (Gerber) doesn’t have that anonymity,” Crawford said. “But she also understands that it does open maybe some doors.”
Gerber spoke to Vogue about what it has been like growing up in the public eye due to her mother.

“Fame was something that I was born into, so I didn’t experience what it was like to become famous,” Gerber said. “I kind of thought that my way of being raised was the most anonymous it could get under the circumstances, and then I met Homer. Like, there are no photos of him as a child online, whereas my entire childhood and teenage years are on the internet. I can only imagine. I’m 24 but … very interviewed.”
Gerber began modeling at 13 and was walking runways at 16, according to Vogue.

“I’ve only ever been a nepo baby, and I’ve only ever benefited in my career from it,” she said “But I also find myself doing it to other nepo babies, thinking, like, OK, show me why you deserve this job. I said to Homer — because the concept is daunting to him, having lived as an adult so far without that perception, whereas I sort of went through it when I wasn’t fully sentient — I said to him, ‘Homer, unfortunately with this show, it’s not like you’re just any unknown actor and people will judge you as an unknown actor.’”
Homer Gere did not begin acting professionally until appearing in a small role in the final season of HBO’s “Euphoria” earlier this year.
“I didn’t grow up in the industry at all,” he told Vogue. “I had never been on a professional set until last summer.”
He and Gerber also didn’t ignore their unique connection when they both joined the cast of “The Shards.”
“Twenty minutes into knowing each other, I was like, ‘Should we just acknowledge the fact that our parents were married?’ She was like, ‘Yeah. Cool,’” he told Vogue. “And that was it.”

title: AARP’s List of ‘Most Fabulous’ Gen X Actresses Honors Viola Davis and More Hollywood Stars
summary: Viola Davis leads AARP’s Movies for Grownups’ 25 Most Fabulous Gen X Actresses list.
story: Viola Davis is fabulous!

The Oscar winner tops AARP’s Movies for Grownups’ 25 Most Fabulous Gen X Actresses list, which “honors powerhouse female talent who continue to break barriers, command screens, and redefine what it means to be a Gen X actress in Hollywood,” according a news release.
The rankings pay homage to Generation X, which is classified as people born between roughly 1965 and 1980.

“Now, at roughly between the ages of 45 to 61, this generation of Hollywood actresses have not faded from the screen, but have built production companies, developed their own projects, and reinvented themselves behind the camera as directors, producers, and entrepreneurs fighting for equal pay and breaking stereotypes,” AARP’s Movies for Grownups said in a statement.
“They are far from slowing down and are doing the most ambitious work of their careers.”

Davis, 61, is the oldest person on the list and said in a statement connected to the honor, “My ability to overcome and to challenge and to believe in my ability is mine.” She survived a poor childhood marked by food insecurity to emerge as a critically acclaimed actor, winning a best supporting actress Academy Award for “Fences” and earning three other nominations in her career.

“When you come to Hollywood, I think women over 40, then over 50, you feel like you’ve just sort of disappeared and fallen off a cliff,” she told AARP’s Movies for Grownups. “Like you’re invisible. So, it’s nice to know that that’s not true. I feel like my value is going up. It feels fabulous.”

title: Elizabeth Acevedo Shares First Page of Novel in Verse, ‘Anger Is Only a Shadow’
summary: Elizabeth Acevedo previews the first page of her novel in verse “Anger Is Only a Shadow” and explains how it sets up the rest of her book.
story: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a good story starts with a good first line. In TODAY’s “Cold Open,” authors tease their buzzy upcoming release by revealing and explaining its first line, paragraph or page.

Either because of her own lactose intolerance, or her memory of what lunch would smell like at the detention center she used to teach at, Elizabeth Acevedo knew her next novel would open with the “visceral” image of indigestion.
“Here is the most important rule of this place: Don’t drink the milk,” reads the opening line of her novel in verse “Anger Is Only a Shadow,” out Sept. 15 from HarperCollins.

The book’s narrator is a rebellious young woman named Lil, who finds herself in juvenile detention due to her “instinct for freedom,” per the novel’s premise, inspired by Acevedo’s own experience working as a teaching artist at a detention facility in Washington, D.C.
“It felt like such a visceral image to begin with, this disruption of your bodily functions in a space where that is very much monitored and very much like, not OK,” Acevedo tells TODAY.com.
The first page of the book is Lil “emphasizing the rules of this place,” both to herself and to the reader. Following the heading of, “Sunday, October 18,” it reads:

Here is the most important rule of this place: Don’t drink the milk. Trust, having the bubble guts is not the first impression you want to make. And while we’re on the subject, that’s an important rule too: don't make an impression.

Sit quiet, only slump so much in your chair, don’t look anyone in the face. Don’t avoid someone eyeing you either. And if you have to make an impression, let it be knuckle-size. Aldwin has been teaching me since I was little: know when to be brick-built, know when to be gentle. And here? Being soft don’t play here.

There are other rules you need to learn: Which YDR—youth development representative—you can joke with. When it makes sense to participate in an activity, or when it makes sense to stay your flat ass behind your door. What vent carries your voice into other units.
But the most important rule is Rule One: Don't. Drink. The. Milk.
The first page of the novel represents what Acevedo pictured her novel in verse to be. And the Lil readers meet through that introduction is the same way Acevedo found the character.

“I thought I was writing a book about a juvenile detention facility and this young woman who is in there and is kind of snarky and telling us the rules,” she says. “The first page was such a guide in her voice, really.

“Before I had plot, before I knew what the main conflict was, I was just kind of following the most irreverent character I’ve ever written,” she adds. “I knew I had a character long before I knew I had anything else.”

The rest came later, including its structure. Acevedo originally thought the novel would be entirely prose poetry, consisting of “blocky text without paragraph indentation.” In the final draft, the prose blocks, accompanied by dates, guide readers through Lil’s daily life. These entries are broken up by poems.

Acevedo first drafted a poem in Lil’s voice titled “Where I’m From.” It sparked a motif, and the character turns one writing prompt from a workshop at the detention center into a series of poems, illustrating how she’s “revising versions of herself,” Acevedo says.
When Acevedo worked as a teaching artist, she says she brought in poems.

“It’s a fraught space,” she says of her time teaching at a detention center. “You come in, and you’re like, ‘Let’s be really vulnerable in a space where you all are very reluctant to share vulnerability.’

“That tension was so visceral for me, and also ... the young women would open up in ways I had never imagined,” she adds. “It’s almost like I was constantly surprised and also fully understood like, ‘You have been looking for an opportunity for people to ask you these things.’”
But the book isn’t just about Lil’s time in the detention center. The novel also asks: “What are the stakes once you’re outside?”
“Anger Is Only a Shadow” will also follow Lil once she’s on probation, weighed down by an ankle monitor and fearing for her big brother, miles away at college.

“So many young people I know when I was a school teacher had ankle monitors, and how does that affect how you navigate your life? And what would be the thing that would lead this character, who’s very impulsive, to potentially violate the rules of the ankle monitor?” Acevedo says. “That’s when the second part of the story, a story I never thought I would write about, came forth.”
The result is “two big stories” rolled into the novel: one about juvenile detention and one about navigating a family member who has mental illness.

“I have a sibling who was diagnosed with schizophrenia when I was in the early years of my college career,” she says. “Trying to do well in my own little world of academics, while also showing up for family, and the ways in which it can be so hard to know what that person needs ... It felt like I just have so many questions about this. I don’t have answers.
“Then that felt like the challenge: Isn’t that exactly what you need to write about?” she continues.

“I’m not going to lie, I wasn’t sure,” she adds. “These are two big stories and I’m writing a very short book, I don’t think it can happen. But somehow, somehow, it felt like the two pieces were supposed to be interlocked.”

title: Harry Styles Announces 2027 Dates for ‘Together, Together’ Tour In 12 New Cities
summary: Harry Styles is adding 25 dates across 12 cities in 2027 to his “Together, Together” tour.
story: Harry Styles is adding more dates to his “Together, Together Tour.” The singer announced Sept. 10 that he will perform 25 concerts in 12 cities in 2027 that will span North America and Europe.
The new dates will begin April 2 in Phoenix, Arizona, and wrap Aug. 28 in London.

“When we decided to do the 2026 tour I knew it would be special but what you turned it into was far beyond what I could have imagined,” Styles said in an email to fans Sept. 9. “I love playing music, I love being with all of you and being a part of the love and joy you all create together every night. That’s why I wanted you to be the first to know we will be adding 2027 dates.”
In that letter to fans, Styles spoke of “what comes next” for him after touring, which led fans to speculate about its meaning.

Styles’ “Together Together Tour” launched in May with 67 shows in Amsterdam, London, São Paulo, Mexico City, New York, Melbourne and Sydney. He is in the midst of a 30-night residence at New York City’s Madison Square Garden, for what are currently his only stop in the U.S.
Tour information can be found at Styles’ website. General sale of tickets for North American dates begins Sept. 16 at 9 a.m. local time.

title: Please Don’t Destroy’s Martin Herlihy Leaves ‘SNL’ After Five Years
summary: Martin Herlihy, comedy writer and of Please Don’t Destroy fame, is leaving “Saturday Night Live” after five years on the NBC sketch comedy show.
story: Martin Herlihy is leaving “Saturday Night Live” after five years on the NBC sketch comedy show.
The comedian, a writer for the program who’s also appeared in dozens of sketches, is not returning for the next season, he has confirmed.

Herlihy debuted on “SNL” in 2021 as part of comedy trio Please Don’t Destroy with fellow comedians Ben Marshall and John Higgins. The group, who produced pre-recorded digital shorts for the show, drew a significant following for their absurdist humor. Their most memorable sketches include one in which former cast member Pete Davidson features them in a music video about “Three Sad Virgins,” featuring Taylor Swift.

In another, the crew, along with actor Brendan Gleeson, play a couple of juniors who are looking forward to their final year of high school. Things go awry when Gleeson reveals that he is, in fact, a 67-year-old Irishman.

The trio’s time together on the comedy program came to an end in 2025, following Season 50. Herlihy, who has also appeared in his own solo digital shorts, remained a writer while Higgins left the show. Marshall was promoted to cast member. Please Don’t Destroy, however, has continued to perform together outside of the NBC show and is currently on tour.

Herlihy — whose father is longtime Adam Sandler collaborator Tim Herlihy, who was also once a head writer on “SNL” — joins several other recent big-name departures from the sketch comedy program. Most recently, Chloe Fineman announced in July that she would not be returning for the 52nd season.

“It’s really hard to leave ‘SNL’ but it does feel like the right time,” Fineman, who spent seven seasons on the series, wrote on Instagram. “I’m going to miss it a lot. But the people who work there are my family and that place is my home, and I know I’ll never be too far away.”

title: Kaya Scodelario Responds to Speculation That Meghan Markle Is Joining ‘The Gentlemen’
summary: Kaya Scodelario is responding to speculation about Meghan Markle will be making an appearance in the next season of “The Gentlemen.”
story: Kaya Scodelario is responding to speculation about Meghan Markle will be making an appearance in the next season of “The Gentlemen.”
“The more the merrier. Everyone, come have a go,” she said during an appearance on the 3rd Hour of TODAY on Sept. 9.
In an Aug. 21 article, Variety reported that Markle was in talks to join the third season of “The Gentlemen,” Guy Ritchie’s Netflix show.
Scodelario said she has no say in the matter, but she is following the news.
“I, unfortunately, have no decision-making abilities. I wish I did. I would love to cast the show myself. I’d put all my friends in it,” she said.
The hit Netflix series just dropped its second season and was renewed for a third.

“I think what’s wonderful about our show is that we have these characters pop up and we get these great guest actors come in, sprinkle a little bit of their magic into the characters and make really memorable scenes out of them. It’s one of the things I love most about the show,” Scodelario said.
According to IMDB, “The Gentlemen” has filmed in locations in the United Kingdom.
Markle recently moved back to the United Kingdom with her husband Prince Harry and their two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, after living in the United States for several years.

Before meeting Prince Harry, Markle starred on the USA Network series “Suits” for seven seasons. After stepping back from her formal duties as a royal in 2020, Markle ventured into reality TV. She starred in two seasons of a lifestyle Netflix series titled “With Love, Meghan.”
Markle and Prince Harry also starred in a six-part Netflix docuseries “Harry & Meghan,” which featured intimate interviews and never-before-seen footage of the couple.
In 2022, Markle spoke with Variety and shared whether she’d ever return to acting.
“No. I’m done,” she said at the time. “I guess never say never, but my intention is to absolutely not.”

title: Gal Gadot Says She’s ‘Trying to Navigate’ AI and Hollywood ‘The Best Way I Can’
summary: Gal Gadot spoke about the use of AI for the movie Bitcoin and why she is defending it.
story: As conversation around artificial intelligence use in Hollywood continues to evolve, some celebrities have weighed in. Now, Gal Gadot is throwing her hat in the ring.
The actor, who stopped by Studio 1A Sept. 9 to discuss her new film “The Runner,” will soon appear in a movie called about the origins of Bitcoin.
While chatting with Gadot, TODAY’s Craig Melvin asked how the star felt about “Bitcoin” using AI for several elements of production.
“And you’re OK with this?” he asked.
Gadot acknowledged that it’s a “complex subject.”
She then shared her own take on the matter.
“AI is here and the train has left the station and it’s happening. Am I afraid of it? Am I scared of it? Yes. Am I going to look away and avoid it? No,” she said.
Rather than living in fear of AI, the actor said she’s trying to embrace it while remaining cautious.
“I’m curious to learn about AI’s benefits and hopefully without replacing humanity,” she said.
Craig then brought up the fear that AI will take human jobs, including in Hollywood, and asked what Gadot thought about the topic.
“I don’t know. I hope not. The same thing was said back in the day about moving to digital and CGI and all these things,” she said. “The truth is, I have no idea. I’m only an actress.”
“I try to navigate the best way I can,” she said.

“Bitcoin” also stars Casey Affleck, Pete Davidson and Isla Fisher. A story about the film’s production in “The Wrap” explains that it was shot on a soundstage with the set to later be filled in using AI.

Producer Ryan Kavanaugh told the publication part of the decision to use AI was because the movie is set across 200 locations. “We realized we could bring down the cost by utilizing some of the AI tools out there,” he said.

Kavanaugh also spoke about the movie’s use of AI in a LinkedIn post about the movie: “So proud of what we are doing, helping to use AI in a way that empowers creative and helps the industry move forward.”
The use of AI in Hollywood has been a hot topic. Over the summer, AI actor Tilly Norwood landed her first movie role in a film called “Misaligned,” a coming-of-age story about a girl AI bot.
Tilly’s creator, Eline Van der Velden, spoke to NBC News and denied that that AI actor’s role in the film would take work away from human actors.
“Because we would never be making a feature film, so we would never have been casting,” she said.
In July, Netflix also made headlines when the streaming service recreated the late actor Gene Wilder’s voice using AI for a reality series, with permission from his wife and estate.

Back in April, a trailer for the film “As Deep as the Grave” debuted and featured an AI-generated version of the late actor Val Kilmer. The star’s daughter gave permission for him to appear in the film.

Taylor Swift is one of several stars who have taken steps to protect her voice and likeness amid an increasing use of AI. In April, the singer filed trademark applications for two audio clips of her voice. She also filed a third trademark for an image of herself onstage.

title: Hallmark Stars and Fans Have 1 Thing in Common: They Can’t Get Enough. Here’s Why
summary: The stars and fans of the Hallmark Channel explain the network’s enduring appeal on the network’s 25th anniversary.
story: The Hallmark Channel wants to take you on a journey. Maybe it’s a dazzling getaway around the world, or back in time to another era. But the network promises its movies and TV shows will always leave you in a better place.

Whether set in idyllic small towns, merry Christmas destinations, or behind the scenes of famous places like The Plaza, Biltmore Estate, NFL stadiums, and Dollywood, the Hallmark Channel’s offerings are united in their escapism.

In these movies, old flames aren’t red flags but the right guy, finally at the right time. Family mysteries are deciphered with catharsis. Crimes are solved in cozy whodunits. Heartbreak is healed right as new love waltzes in.

That same magic was brought to The 92nd Street Y in New York on Aug. 4. for the network’s 25-year celebration, where Hallmark stars celebrated a quarter century of feel-good television with a sold-out, in-person crowd and virtual audience.
Twenty-two stars and executives gathered together for what they said felt like the ultimate family reunion, and TODAY.com was there to speak to them on the red carpet.

“You look around the room, and it’s just like all these beautiful people that you love working with,” said Marilu Henner, who has worked for the network since 2011 and starred in the “Aurora Teagarden Mysteries” series.

She was standing next to Andie MacDowell, who recently starred in “The Way Home” series, and whose first movie was a Hallmark Hall of Fame film that aired on CBS, “Riding the Bus with My Sister” in 2005.
“Andie and I were like, “Oh, she played my daughter. Oh, he played my daughter’s boyfriend,” Henner added.
Actor Victor Webster, a member of the Hallmark family since 2012, compared the evening to “hanging out with cousins at Christmas.”
“We really look forward to spending time with each other and we value each other,” he added, standing arm-and-arm with Hallmark alum Rachel Boston.

Boston, whose first movie was, “A Ring By Spring” in 2014, said the actors have “the same desire to uplift each other and look to the positive things, and just support each other through challenging times in our lives.”
The Hallmark Channel launched on Aug. 5, 2001. Since then, the network has expanded programming and in 2024 launched their streaming service Hallmark+.

Darren Abbott, President of Hallmark Media and Hallmark Chief Brand Officer told TODAY.com, “25 years ago, someone would have said Hallmark is a greeting card company. Today, we’re so much more than the products we make or the content that we create. We’re really a caring and connecting brand. It’s all about putting goodness and love back in the world.”
What Keeps the Actors Coming Back
“When you hear Hallmark, you just think about love,” said B.J. Britt, standing with “The Groomsmen” trilogy co-stars Heather Hemmens and Tyler Hynes.
What stands out to Erin Cahill, who joined the network in 2016, is the type of love that is captured in Hallmark films — friendship, familial, romantic and self-love.

The longevity in the projects is what keeps Wes Brown, whose first film was “Love Begins,” 2011 and Benjamin Ayres, who stars in “Hope Valley: 1874,” a Hallmark+ exclusive prequel series to “When Calls The Heart,” which is filming its 14th season, coming back for more.
Hallmark’s actors, who often star in multiple films and series, say the casts form lasting bonds.

“I think it’s much like the heartwarming communities that we get to portray in the movies. It’s become a real-life thing,” Lacey Chabert, who has made 45 movies and two series for the network, shared.

“It’s very rare in this industry to have such supportive people with you all the time,” added Scott Michael Foster, standing next to Chabert, his co-star in the exclusive Hallmark+ limited series “Paris Is Always a Good Idea.”

The stories’ meaningful plots lead to a familial environment, sometimes literally. Hallmark veteran Alison Sweeney’s daughter Megan Sweeney made her acting debut alongside her mom in the Hallmark Channel original movie “Romance at Hope Ranch.” Ashley Williams, wrote her latest movie, “Much About Love,” with her husband Neal Dodson.
Another reason for loyalty? Hallmark Media has provided pathways for actors to not only star in movies and series, but also work behind the scenes as writers, producers and directors.

Kimberley Sustad, who recently starred in “Absolutely Devoted to You,” wrote the “Three Wise Men and a Baby” trilogy, alongside Paul Campbell. The first movie made history as cable’s most-watched movie of 2022 with 3.6 million viewers. It ranked second to Paramount network’s “Yellowstone,” per Variety.

Having three male leads wasn’t the norm for Hallmark, and Sustad told TODAY.com the project wouldn’t have come to life without the support of the network. Sustad said she feels lucky “to write things that matter to people and that make people laugh and feel love and hope.”

The impact continues behind the scenes with the “Make Her Mark” women’s directing program. Founded by actor Ashley Williams in 2023, the initiative aims to increase representation of women behind the camera through on-the-job mentorship. Crystal Lowe was the first person to go through the program and is directing her eighth movie.
“It was just time to get more women behind the camera. It’s not just about employing women, it’s about setting them up for success,” Williams said.
Add to Google
Add to Google

The collaboration that Hallmark Media encourages also frequently allows stars to incorporate important personal topics into their projects. Holly Robinson Peete, whose eldest son has autism, was able to executive produce and star in the first autism themed Christmas movie, “Our Christmas Journey” in 2021.

“For someone like me, who’s been doing television since the ‘80s, it’s very rare to find a place that you feel invests in you as a talent, and you know you’re going to work with them forever,” said Robinson Peete.

Another one of Williams’ movies, “Falling Together,” was the first to feature the Walk to End Alzheimer’s in a movie. She added a personal touch by including photos to honor her mother Linda, who had dementia, and fellow Hallmark stars, “Kentucky Roses” Andrew Walker’s mother Joyce, who had Alzheimer’s disease, and Nikki DeLoach’s father David, who had dementia.
Hallmark movies continue to feature meaningful subjects such as Parkinson’s disease, Down syndrome, IVF, foster care, adoption, divorce and cancer.

The love stories are changing, too. The first ever gay Christmas movie was Hallmark’s “The Christmas House,” in 2020, starring Jonathan Bennett. His jacket and the script are now in the Smithsonian as part of the LGBTQ+ archives.

“The biggest part about being a part of Hallmark Channel is getting to tell stories, love stories that reflect a love like mine, Bennett shared with TODAY.com. “To become so ingrained in the fabric of Hallmark Channel and LGBTQ stories has been so amazing and uplifting.”

People will come up to Bennett and tell him how meaningful his work is, “I’ll have a gay couple come up and be like, “Thank you for making that. We feel so seen. I mean, it’s just the best job in the world. I get to tell love stories on the greatest network of love.”
What Keeps the Fans Coming Back
Fans filled 92NY wearing custom T-shirts of their favorite Hallmark heartthrobs, “happy birthday” headbands, heart-shaped sunglasses, Hallmark pins, and jewelry featured in Hallmark films and more.

When superfans and sisters Anne Burger and Kathy Koabel, and their friend Cindy Francis, who saw some of the stars four times in 10 days, were asked about their custom 25th birthday T-shirts and headbands, they said in harmony, “We have to match. It’s Hallmark’s birthday. It’s like family.”

The Hallmark Channel fandom is a key part of the phenomenon. Hallmark Channel was ranked the most-watched network among women by the fourth quarter of the year for the 12th year in a row, according to Forbes.

“I can go anywhere in the world and meet someone who comes up to me with shining eyes to tell us what these movies mean in their life,” Autumn Reeser, who made her debut in “Love at the Thanksgiving Day Parade” in 2012, told TODAY.com.

Niall Matter, who starred in “Christmas at Dollywood” with Dolly Parton, said that fans often share how Hallmark films provide comfort when it comes to dealing with loss, especially at Christmas time.

When asked why she keeps watching after 25 years, fan Gwen Mordecai said, “The movies are magical, especially if you love travel, but also transports you to the kind of family and love that everybody wants to have.”
Hallmark Media creates community and connection, as Mordecai attended the 92NY event with fellow fan and friend Kim Caprio, who she met at a Hallmark store in upstate New York.
Sisters Samara and Ellie Miller were first hooked on Hallmark after watching with their mother. “It’s more than just Christmas movies. We’re all year-round watchers,” Samara Miller said.
Leaning into the fandom, Hallmark has started interactive experiences with the stars, the Christmas Experience at their headquarters in Kansas City, Missouri and the Christmas Cruise in 2024.

Last year, 200,000 people attended the Christmas Experience and the cruise was so popular it inspired the series “Christmas at Sea.” This summer, the inaugural Hallmark Stars Live bus tour hosted by 11 year Hallmark Channel fixture Nikki DeLoach, kicked off in New Jersey and wrapped in Nebraska.
Fan Barbara Chartier called the Hallmark Stars Live show she attended in Rhode Island a “true pinch-me moment.”
“There aren’t any Hollywood stars that can hold a candle to the Hallmark stars. They think nothing of making their fans feel special,” she said.
“What you see is what you get. They live and breathe the Hallmark brand. You feel the authenticity,” stated Annie Howell, CCO of Hallmark Media.

In true Hallmark fashion, Chartier met a mother and daughter waiting in line. As fate would have it their seats were near each other. They have kept in touch, and she considers them to be lifelong friends.
For fans, Hallmark programming is a happy diversion from the stresses of daily life.
DeLoach told the crowd in Rhode Island, “Even in our darkest days, when we are in our valleys, we are reaching for the light.”

“It isn’t just a television show. It isn’t just a great performance. It is what people take away. They feel like they’ve changed a little bit because they spent time with the Hallmark brand,” said Michelle Vicary, Head of Programming at Hallmark Media.
Barbara Niven, who received her SAG card from a Hallmark Hall of Fame movie and has worked with Hallmark for 23 years, nearly its entire existence, says the network’s appeal is not surprising.
“In this world that needs positive energy, Hallmark creates that, and I think we remind people that there is good out there, and that people can be good and kind and loving.”

title: Director of Mr. T Documentary Marvels at How the Cultural Icon Became a ‘Superhero’
summary: “Untold Mr. T: I Pity the Fool” director Scott Weintrob speaks with TODAY.com about Mr. T’s rise to fame and what makes him so compelling.
story: Let’s conduct an experiment: Close your eyes and think of the 1980s. In the diorama of your mind, maybe you’re seeing Jordache jeans, Ferris Bueller or Pac-Man. They’re all fine and dandy, but, come on, how could you not think of Mr. T?

Mr. T, born Laurence Tureaud, is the quintessential American success story of the decade, a star who is the subject of the Netflix documentary, “Untold Mr. T: I Pity the Fool,” premiering Sept. 8, which chronicles his improbable rise to fame, while taking viewers back to the peak of his popularity.
“This movie is a nostalgia bomb,” director Scott Weintrob tells TODAY.com.

It is, and it’s so much more, peeling back the layers of how Mr. T actually became Mr. T. One of 12 children, he grew up in a Chicago ghetto. Adorned with a display window’s supply of necklaces around his neck, along with earrings, sunglasses and a shocking mohawk, he burst on the scene opposite Sylvester Stallone as the villainous Clubber Lang in 1982’s “Rocky III.”
The documentary traces his evolution and looks back at a defining moment of his youth when his mother was robbed and he sought retribution.
“Mr. T had a situation that he faced after his mother was attacked that turned him into what we know as Mr. T, their superhero,” Weintrob says.

The documentary also dives into the etymology of his self-given moniker and how fame found him. After the incident with his mother, he became a bodyguard and was eventually cast in “Rocky III,” before landing the part of B.A. Baracus in “The A-Team,” an NBC action series that became a big hit.

Mr. T was a superstar. A cartoon series followed. Stickers. Breakfast cereal. Action figures. Endorsement deals out the yin yang. He got in on the movement to not do drugs. And, of course, there’s the catch phrase. “I pity the fool” was as ubiquitous as his muscles.
“Mr. T was so famous. He had fame that people today just don’t even understand because everybody watched the show,” Weintrob says of “The A-Team.”

It’s easy to dismiss Mr. T as a character from the decade of decadence, but that’s not fair. As the documentary explores, he’s always been interested in raising up the downtrodden. He just happened to blaze a trail for others in the process.
“He did set the standard for so many artists to dress how they wanted to dress, dress loud, be noticed,” Weintrob says.

“Mr. T told me that Muhammad Ali always told him, ‘Stand out. You need to stand out if you want to be noticed.’ And I feel like we live in a generation now of young kids trying to stand out and be noticed … This is a different time, and it was all about being yourself. And he was one of the first.”

“The A-Team” offered Mr. T a chance to change the narrative after his menacing turn in “Rocky III.” He was still enormous and tough, but also human, as evidenced by the recurring bit on the show that addressed his character’s fear of flying. After “The A-Team” came out, he crossed the bridge from terrifying to teddy bear, one of the 1980s most memorable personalities.

“He was the right person at the right time,” Weintrob says. “Remember, when TV was so focused on just a few shows that everybody watched them, when Mr. T walked onto the screen, everybody was like, ‘Who is that?’ We’d never seen anyone quite like him.
“There’s a bravery to that. There’s a bravery to putting yourself out there in a way that people may criticize, and he didn’t care. He was always going to be the person that he believed in.”
There’s a bravery to putting yourself out there in a way that people may criticize, and he didn’t care. He was always going to be the person that he believed in.
Scott Weintrob on Mr. t
Today, you can watch what you want when you want, on any number of platforms, a far cry from how the world worked when “The A-Team” was on. The options were limited, which worked out for Mr. T.

“You were given one or two or three or four clear streams of entertainment, and you watched them when they were on, and that was that. And Mr. T was the champion,” Weintrob says. “There was no one else quite like him at the time, and there’s still no one else quite like him today.”
In an era when audiences were presented with characters — think Alf or Pee-Wee Herman — Mr. T was authentic.
“He was Mr. T onscreen and Mr. T offscreen. He was the same character, and people were just so shocked by it,” Weintrob says.
“Mr. T is an incredible human. There’s only one Mr. T. There’ll never ever be another like him,” he adds.
Singular in nature, Mr. T still elicits a reaction among people, one that Weintrob wants to bring out in “Untold.”

“I hope viewers watch this and come away with it and feel good,” he says. “I hope they feel happy. There’s an emotion that comes with watching the film, and if you don’t feel anything at the end, well, it probably wasn’t the right film for you.”

It’s been more than 40 years since “Rocky III” and the premiere of “The A-Team.” Mr. T remains as beloved today as he ever was. Sure, there’s some nostalgia, but he remains dedicated to uplifting others.

“Going out to dinner with Mr. T is a very lengthy experience because it takes him 25 minutes to get from the door to the table because he talks to everybody. Everybody comes up to him. He loves everybody, and everyone loves him,” Weintrob says.

Mr. T, in an interview with The Guardian published Sept. 3, disavowed the documentary, saying it focused too much on his stereotypical image. “If you don’t know me, you’re gonna think I’m some monster,” the documentary quoted him as saying.

Weintrob, in an interview with TV Insider published Sept. 8, responded to the criticism, saying he had a different takeaway from his film’s subject. He said the last time he saw Mr. T was at a screening: “He loved it. He cried, he hugged us.”
“These words of he doesn’t like it. I don’t even know where they even came from. They sound like untruths,” he said.

“Is it heartbreaking that a journalist says that Mr. T doesn’t like it? Not in the slightest. What is exciting is we’ve made a film that’s brilliant, really exciting about someone that people can be inspired by,” he continued.

title: The Opening Line of Alice Hoffman’s ‘The Witches of Cambridge’ Is Also How It Ends
summary: Alice Hoffman previews the beginning of “The Witches of Cambridge,” her new book which was chosen as a Read With Jenna pick.
story: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a good story starts with a good first line. In TODAY’s “Cold Open,” authors tease their buzzy upcoming release by revealing and explaining its first line, paragraph or page.
Alice Hoffman, author of the “Practical Magic” series, is back with another book about witches, but they’re not the Owens sisters.
“The Witches of Cambridge,” out Sept. 8 and named as Read with Jenna’s September pick, unfolds at a secret society for witches at Radcliffe College in the 1950s.

Ava, unaware of her magical heritage, and Lauren, who is extremely aware of hers, both come to terms with their powers and legacies against the backdrop of the Red Scare. As Joseph McCarthy’s witch hunts play out miles away in Washington, D.C. Lauren and Ava explore the lingering presence of the Salem Witch Trials in their own lives and in Cambridge.
The book opens with an evocative sentence about Ava’s isolated childhood in Maine, where she was raised by parents who wanted to hem her in and deny her magic.
In every story there is a beginning, and this was hers, the one she had been waiting for all her life.
“That’s the way I want my life to open,” Hoffman tells TODAY.com, laughing.

In a way, Hoffman’s life reads like a story. She grew up in a single-parent, working-class household. A self-described “secret writer,” Hoffman never thought she could become an author, and she nearly dropped out of high school. Her older brother, studying in California, encouraged her to attend college. Her writing career unfolded fast while at Stanford: She won a writing award and published her first novel at 21. Since then, she has published 30 books.
Ava’s life also opens when she goes to college.

“Ava going off from Maine to have a different life, she doesn’t really know who she is. She goes off to Cambridge and she’s with people very different than she grew up with. This is the beginning for her,” she says.
Hoffman had a second college experience, one that inspired “The Witches of Cambridge,” when she decided to study at the Harvard Divinity School.

“I was surrounded by younger people with so much kind of hope. It was definitely their beginnings,” she says. “I felt very influenced by being with a lot of young people who were searching and looking to kind of restart their lives.”
“The Witches of Cambridge” follows a four-year college experience, and then some, for Lauren and Ava. But it doesn’t end with an ending. Hoffman says the first line echoes the last line of the book.
All you had to do was begin.
Their lives are cyclical: right when one chapter ends, another begins. Hoffman feels she isn’t done following their story, and is currently at work on a sequel.
“I feel like it could end where it did, but there’s so much more that could happen,” she says.

title: Should Celebrities With Dance Backgrounds Be on ‘DWTS’? Mark Ballas Shares His Thoughts
summary: “Dancing With the Stars” pro Mark Ballas reacts to celebrities with dance backgrounds competing on the show.
story: “Take It From Me” is a TODAY.com series where experts use their wisdom to explain trends or make recommendations within their fields. In this latest installment, “Dancing With the Stars” pro Mark Ballas breaks down celebrities with dance backgrounds competing on the show.
Every year after a new “Dancing With the Stars” cast is announced, fans have varying opinions about the latest celebrities vying for the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy — and this year is no different.

Sixteen stars will be competing on Season 35 of the competition show, some with past dance experience. Among them is Julia Stiles, known for her moves in “Save the Last Dance,” and Jenna Dewan and Harry Shum Jr., who are both trained dancers.
Some social media users have been criticizing their casting, arguing that they have an advantage over other celebrities with no prior experience.
But “DWTS” pro Mark Ballas has a different take.

“The show’s called ‘Dancing With the Stars,’ not ‘Dancing With the Stars With No Dance Experience,’” he tells TODAY.com. “Good luck casting 12 to 16 people in the entertainment industry, and one of them hasn’t danced before.”
The 40-year-old dancer and three-time Mirrorball champ also notes that dance experience is not always an advantage.

“It’s about finding teams that you’re invested in. The cool thing about the show is it’s all about preference, right?” he says before mentioning the voting process that determines which couples remain on the show every episode.
The different skill level, he says, is what makes “DWTS” exciting and keeps viewers tuning in.

“If you had a whole show of complete and utter beginners who can’t dance at all, that’s not fun. And if you have it the other way, with all dancers, that’s not as fun either,” Ballas continues. “But it’s fun to see great dances. It’s fun to see people struggle and then overcome the struggle. And it’s fun to see people who are like, ‘Oh wait, how come you’re, like, accidentally pretty good at this?’”
He adds that what’s great about “DWTS” is that “it feeds every different viewer for what they want to see.”
Carrie Ann Inaba, who has been a judge since the first season, also chimed in on the debate. She explained that it matters what previous dance styles a celebrity has tried before being cast.

“What’s difficult — and I don’t think people realize this — is when you go from being a jazz dancer or a hip-hop dancer or all the other forms of dancing (to ballroom),” she told Entertainment Weekly. “The weight placement is so different. It’s weird because your body has memory, so it remembers how to dance, and it thinks it already knows how to do these moves, but it doesn’t.”
She added, “It takes a lot of time to un-train the body to put your weight on the front more over your toes instead of back and down and grounded.”
“It’s not as easy as people think,” Inaba said, pointing out that the advantage some dancers have is based on their rhythm and musicality.

Going into his 22nd season, and this time with fellow “Traitors” alum Maura Higgins as his partner, Ballas tells TODAY.com he just wants his partners to “feel like they got the best experience that they possibly could.”

“It’s a once in a lifetime experience. And think about it, it’s quite silly, we’re ballroom dancing on telly and you get a new style every six days, and you’re just hoping that you make it to the end,” he shares.
The new season of “Dancing With the Stars” premieres Sept. 15, with a second episode on Sept. 16.

title: What Happened in the Elizabeth Holmes Doc, According to Someone Who Saw It
summary: Here’s what the Elizabeth Holmes documentary was like according to a person who was at a screening at Sundance.
story: “Catch Me Up” is a TODAY series where our experts and journalists bring readers up to speed on the day’s biggest headlines.
A surprise documentary about Theranos founder and convicted felon Elizabeth Holmes has created instant buzz after a screening at a film festival and the release of a trailer that has gone viral.

Rebecca Keegan of NBC News Digital was in attendance at the Telluride Film Festival in Colorado when the documentary “You Can See Everything” was screened on Sept. 7. The film was directed by absurdist comedian Nathan Fielder and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim and produced jaw-dropping reactions from those in the crowd.
“There were audible gasps and ‘no ways’ consistently throughout this almost three-hour film,” Keegan told NBC News correspondent Erin McLaughlin on TODAY Sept. 8.

Holmes was the founder and CEO of the tech startup Theranos, which promised to revolutionize blood testing. She was found guilty of four counts of wire fraud in January 2022 after a federal investigation uncovered critical violations in a Theranos lab following reports that the technology did not work and could deliver faulty results.

The new documentary, which will be released in October, features footage of Holmes and partner Billy Evans with their two children at a rental home in San Diego before Holmes entered federal prison in 2023. She is scheduled to be released in 2031.
“I think part of the film is exploring this question of Elizabeth Holmes’s perception of reality and about things that she’s done,” Keegan said.
A trailer released by the studio A24 on Sept. 7 shows a wide-eyed Holmes awkwardly only inches away from Fielder’s face as she speaks to him in one scene.

“I’m not that person,” Holmes says in the clip. “I can promise you that. I don’t have anything to deceive you on. Of course, I’m not deceiving you. I’m engaging with you as a human being. Why would I deceive you? There’s no reason for me to do that.”
“OK. All right. OK, good chat,” Fielder replies.
The two then stare at each other for an uncomfortable duration.
“You’re being real right now?” Fielder asks.
“I’m always being real,” Holmes replies.
Keegan described a “strange feeling” produced by the interactions between Fielder and Holmes in the film.
“Fielder is very much a character in the film, and in some ways, it’s him trying to understand whether he believes Elizabeth Holmes or not,” Keegan said.

“I’m struggling to this day to understand exactly what I experienced,” Fielder said during the post-screening Q&A, according to Keegan. “I don’t know why they want me there. I’m a weird guy. I don’t get it. That messed with my head.”

The conversations between Holmes and “The Rehearsal” star are reportedly not the only surreal moments in the documentary. The film also includes an A-list Hollywood actress reenacting Fielder’s conversations with Holmes from prison. Fielder asked the attendees at the screening not to reveal the actress’s identity, according to Keegan.
NBC News reached out to Holmes for comment, but did not hear back. Holmes shared the movie trailer on her X account on Sept. 6 and wrote, “I’m always being real.”

“You Can See Everything” is the latest screen adaptation of the saga involving Holmes. HBO released the documentary “The Inventor” about Holmes in 2019, and then Amanda Seyfried played her in the 2022 Hulu series “The Dropout.”

title: Would Sheinelle Ever Join ‘RHONY’? Jenna Gets Answers About that Rumor
summary: Jenna Bush Hager asked Sheinelle Jones if she would consider joining the cast of Bravo’s “The Real Housewives of New York City.”
story: Sheinelle Jones beams into living rooms every day from New York City on TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle, so would she consider adding another iconic New York show to her resume?
On the Sept. 8 episode of the show, Sheinelle and Jenna chatted with the “RHONY” cast, and Jenna mentioned there had a been a rumor that Sheinelle would be one of the housewives on the program.
“By a show of hands, who thinks she should join next season?” Jenna asked, as the entire cast cheered and raised their hands.
“It’s like being in an encouraging classroom,” Sheinelle said.
Jenna then Sheinelle outright: “Would you ever do it?”
“We’re going to keep the suspense,” she said coyly.
“That’s a maybe,” Jenna said.
“There you go,” Sheinelle said.
“You’d be filming all day long,” Jenna said, while Sheinelle asked the cast if cameras were around them 24/7.
“She’s getting some fact finding info,” Jenna said, prompting Sheinelle to laugh.

Sheinelle may not be part of the “Real Housewives” universe, but fans can still check out the 16th season of “RHONY,” which premieres Sept. 8 at 8 p.m. ET on Bravo and streams the next day on Peacock.

The new season will see Season 15 returnees Sai De Silva, Erin Lichy and Jessel Taank joined by Hailey Glassman, Erika Hammond and Daisy Toye. Rounding out the cast is Carole Radziwill, back full-time on the reality show for the first time since 2018’s Season 10.
Radziwill has said her return to the franchise is an “opportunity” after her name appeared in files related the Jeffrey Epstein investigation.

“I mean, I felt like this isn’t something I shy away from,” Radziwill said at a press event Sept. 1. “Me and many, many, many, many more people found their names in these files. And it’s not something I shy away from because I think, really, it’s important to talk about it. It’s important to be transparent. Obviously, I didn’t know anything, as no one, you know, 20 years ago would have known anything.”

title: Sandra Bullock Pries Hoda Kotb for More Details About Her ‘Connection’ With Man on Plane
summary: Sandra Bullock asked Hoda Kotb for more information about he man she met on a plane, sparking talk about a possible love connection.
story: Sandra Bullock turned the tables on Hoda Kotb in order to try and get some intel on her love life.

Hoda sat down with Bullock and Nicole Kidman to discuss their upcoming movie, “Practical Magic 2,” but the “Speed” star wanted to find out more about the mystery man Hoda met on a plane and discussed when she visited TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle on Aug. 21.
Bullock said she saw the segment in which Hoda opened up about the encounter.
“A question was posed to you about a flight that you took, and there was a little conversation and a little sparklet? What happened?” Bullock asked.
“So I was on a plane and I sat next to some guy, and he’s super whatever,” Hoda said.
“Handsome? Super handsome?” Bullock fired back.
Hoda confirmed she and the man swapped phone numbers before they went their separate ways.

“I didn’t know if it was a connection like just a bond for a second, or was it something — I don’t know. I still don’t know,” she said, while Bullock looked at the camera and mouthed the words, “Call her,” promoting Hoda to laugh.
“This is my favorite interview ever,” Hoda howled, as Bullock mouthed “soft skin” while caressing her arm.
“This is intense,” Kidman joked.
“Did you say ‘soft skin’? You are so weird,” Hoda told Bullock.
“Well, that’s important. If you look at someone and you go, ‘Am I going to enjoy touching their very soft skin?’ You will enjoy it,” Bullock replied.

While chatting with Jenna Bush Hager and Sheinelle Jones last month, Hoda divulged details of what seemed like a meet cute with the mystery man, saying their chat on the plane was “firing on all cylinders.” After the flight, the pair bumped into each other again in Cannes while her company Joy 101 was there, and they said hello to each other. They would later text, but Hoda wasn’t sure where things stood. She did confirm the man was single.
“Look. There are connections,” she said. “I don’t know what it is.”

title: Saudi shutdown of key pipeline limits oil flow as Yemen hits back against Houthis
summary: Saudi Arabia has closed a critical oil pipeline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq, the latest squeeze on Middle Eastern supplies after attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels this week threatened to deepen the world’s energy crisis.
story: Saudi Arabia has closed a critical oil pipeline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq, the latest squeeze on Middle Eastern supplies after attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels this week threatened to deepen the world’s energy crisis.

The 745-mile pipeline had helped Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest crude oil exporter, bypass the blocked Strait of Hormuz, through which some 20% of the world’s oil used to pass before the U.S. and Israel waged war on Iran in late February.

The Saudi Energy Ministry confirmed the shutdown of the East-West pipeline on Friday, adding that drone attacks had resulted in a number of injuries and that its teams were “taking the necessary measures to secure the pipeline and assess its safety.”

Saudi Arabia said it would not retaliate for now following a request from Iraq’s prime minister, while reserving the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security and critical facilities, according to a Saudi foreign ministry statement.
The pipeline has been moving 4-5% of global oil supplies, new agency Reuters reported Friday.

An Iraqi military commander was dismissed early on Saturday after investigations confirmed the latest drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia originated from Iraq, according to a statement by Iraq‘s prime minister’s office.
Iraq also closed two key border crossings with Iran, Iraq’s state-run news agency reported Saturday.

Kuwait, a U.S. ally in the region, warned that the pipeline attack was a “dangerous escalation that undermines the security and stability of the region,” while Bahrain stressed Saudi Arabia’s right to “take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty.”

U.S. President Donald Trump said on ⁠Saturday that everything would “work out just ⁠fine” when asked about the region on a visit to Ireland. He also said, without providing evidence, that Iran was “probably” behind the pipeline attack.

The pipeline strikes came as rebel Houthi forces in Yemen captured Perim, an island in the middle of the vital Bab el Mandeb Strait, which serves as a gateway to the Red Sea trade route that links Europe and Asia.

The Houthis also captured the historic port city of Mocha this week, followed by an advance on the strategic coastal town of Dhubab and the apparent withdrawal of forces from the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government from Perim, also known as Mayun.

If the Houthis are able to threaten shipping along the Bab el Mandeb Strait, it could reduce oil supplies through another key waterway. Saudi Arabia has had to rely on the Red Sea route given the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz.
Yemeni Ministry of Defense said Saturday it had carried out counterattacks against Houthi targets, hitting militants, vehicles and weaponry.

A statement issued by Houthi forces on Friday said that “maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels,” vowing to strike Saudi targets “until the aggression stops and the blockade against our dear people is lifted.”
Trump said the Houthis had contacted the U.S. to stress that they “don’t want to fight with us” and would “much prefer not having us involved.”
Oil prices ended the week above $100 a barrel for the first time since Mid-May after the dramatic developments.

Effective Houthi control over the Red Sea coast “is a game changer,” and could give Iran powerful new leverage in its war with the United States, Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics, told NBC News.
He said: “Far from being really besieged and bleeding, Iran now could easily increase the pain to the U.S. economy and the world economy.”
Gerges said it remains to be seen whether the Houthis can maintain their control of the vast areas of the Red Coast, or if they “overextended themselves.”

But the Trump administration “now finds itself in a much more difficult position because it gambled that the blockade of Iran would force Iran to accept Trump’s conditions,” he added. “The reverse has happened.”

Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian said Saturday that it would sign an agreement with Oman over a joint route through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, as part of a deal securing future navigation rights through the strait.
That deal is not expected to immediately reopen the waterway without a broader agreement with the U.S., Iran has previously stressed.

The U.S. military is helping its Saudi counterparts to develop and coordinate targets inside Yemen, according to a U.S. official and a person familiar with the matter, after Saudi Arabia vowed a firm response to hostilities.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman is urging President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, according to a person familiar with the matter. The president and the Crown Prince have discussed the recent escalation by the Houthis at least twice in the last 24 hours, this person said Friday.
The United Nations’ International Organization for Migration warned on Friday at least 46,000 people have so far been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week.
It said that figure spanned the West Coast and Taiz governorates as of Thursday, with the numbers of those displaced “alarmingly rising by the hour.”
The organization called on all parties to the conflict to “guarantee safe humanitarian access and to protect civilians, aid workers and assets on the ground.”

title: Strikes shut down key Saudi pipeline as Iran-backed Houthis tighten grip on crucial shipping lane
summary: Houthi rebels effectively completed a rapid push to take control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline on Friday, tightening their grip on one of the world’s most important shipping routes and delivering a dramatic boost to their backers in Iran.
story: Houthi rebels effectively completed a rapid push to take control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline on Friday, tightening their grip on one of the world’s most important shipping routes and delivering a dramatic boost to their backers in Iran.
At the same time, strikes inside Saudi Arabia forced the shutdown of a critical oil pipeline, the country’s energy ministry confirmed Friday.

Saudi Arabia said drones launched from Iraq attacked its East-West pipeline, but said it would not retaliate for now following a request from Iraq’s prime minister, while reserving the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security and critical facilities, according to a Saudi foreign ministry statement.

An Iraqi military commander was dismissed early on Saturday after investigations confirmed the latest drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia originated from Iraq, according to a statement by Iraq‘s prime minister’s office.

Houthi forces captured Perim, an island in the middle of the vital Bab el Mandeb Strait, several news agencies reported, citing multiple sources. A day earlier, the Houthis captured the historic port city of Mocha.

That was followed by an advance on the strategic coastal town of Dhubab and the apparent withdrawal of forces from the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government, from Perim, also known as Mayun.

The U.S. military is helping its Saudi counterparts to develop and coordinate targets inside Yemen, according to a U.S. official and a person familiar with the matter, after Saudi Arabia vowed a firm response to hostilities.

The Houthis and the opposing coalition have been fighting a civil war since 2014. The conflict has simmered for years but erupted into intense fighting again in recent weeks, raising concerns of a return to all-out war and posing a serious new threat to the global economy.

Effective Houthi control over Bab el Mandeb, a gateway to the Red Sea trade route that links Europe and Asia, could further imperil oil exports while granting Iran powerful new leverage in its war with the United States.

Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, has had to rely on the Red Sea route given the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, through which some 20% of the world’s oil used to pass, since the U.S. and Israel waged war on the Islamic Republic in late February.
If the Houthis are similarly able to threaten shipping along the Bab el Mandeb Strait, it could reduce oil supplies through another key waterway and deepen the world’s energy crisis.

title: Emma Bonino, leader of abortion and divorce battles that changed Italy, dies at 78
summary: Emma Bonino, who rose to political prominence as a leader of campaigns by the Radical Party that legalized abortion and divorce in the 1970s in heavily Roman Catholic Italy, against the objections of the Vatican, has died.
story: ROME — Emma Bonino, who rose to political prominence as a leader of campaigns by the Radical Party that legalized abortion and divorce in the 1970s in heavily Roman Catholic Italy against the objections of the Vatican, has died. She was 78.
Her party of recent years, +Europa, announced her death.

“Her life was a long struggle against everything that denies freedom: against clandestine abortion, world hunger, the stranglehold of party politics, female genital mutilation, punitive justice, genocide, and every form of authoritarianism,” the party said.

Italy’s conservative prime minister Giorgia Meloni paid tribute to Bonino, saying their different backgrounds and perspectives “never prevented me from acknowledging her significance and her role in our nation’s public life.”
“For decades, Emma Bonino has been a strong and recognizable voice in Italian politics, championing her ideas with determination,” Meloni wrote on social media.

Even after the Radicals’ political star faded, Bonino remained a key political figure and human rights campaigner active in Italy for over five decades. She served as a European commissioner for then-Premier Silvio Berlusconi and was a co-founder of the death penalty watchdog Hands Off Cain. But her bid in 1999 to become Italy’s first female president failed.

She remained known to younger generations as a sought-after political pundit, appearing frequently on Italian TV with her sharp wit and cutting insights. After her cancer diagnosis in 2015, she invariably appeared in public wearing colorful headscarves.
Bonino’s passing follows the recent death of several other feminist heroes, including activist Gloria Steinem and poet Robin Morgan.
Challenging the Vatican

Born on March 9, 1948, in Bra — not far from the northwestern Italian city of Turin, where carmaker Fiat’s factory drove the economy — she spent her childhood on a farm, where she was often tasked to pasture pigs, a lifestyle she described as “deadly boring” in a 2023 TV interview.
Bonino first got involved in Italian politics because she wanted to change the law. At 26, she became pregnant and had an abortion, even though it was illegal at that time.

Recalling the experience as one of the most humiliating of her life, in 1975 she was among the founders of the Information Center for Sterilization and Abortion, an organization that provided information and performed abortions before they were legalized.
The following year she was elected to the Italian parliament for the maverick Radical Party, a bastion of anticlericalism, civil libertarianism, feminism, liberalism and radicalism in Italy.
The party proposed itself as the strongest opposition to the Italian political establishment, seen as corrupt and conservative, and to the Catholic Church’s extensive influence on Italian society.

In 1978 abortion was legalized. That particular campaign may have been over, but Bonino had found her vocation: Politics was her life, and she became one of the most active leaders of the Radical Party and its successors.
She held key political roles in Italy and at the EU

A veteran legislator in Italian politics and an activist for various reform policies, she was elected six times as a Lower House lawmaker and two times as a senator. In 2017, she became the leader of +Europa, a liberal, European federalist party slate she launched ahead of the 2018 Italian general election.
An explosive presence in politics during her 50-year-long career, Bonino was one of the few Italian political figures who scored important achievements both at home and internationally.
Bonino won European exposure in a role she owed to then center-right Premier Berlusconi who, in 1995, offered her one of Italy’s two seats in the European Commission.

As a Commissioner she forged the EU’s consumer protection policy and created the European Commission Humanitarian Office, which is now the primary European humanitarian arm. It was this last portfolio, the humanitarian affairs, that she felt most strongly about.
She traveled to war zones — former Yugoslavia, Rwanda, Sudan, Afghanistan — and convinced Europe that humanitarian assistance couldn’t be an excuse for lack of political or military intervention.
In June 1999 she headed a slate named after her — Lista Bonino — at the European elections. It was an overwhelming success: The party got 8.5% of the votes and became Italy’s fourth political force.
Bonino served as foreign minister, trade minister and EU affairs minister in Italian center-left governments of the 2000s and 2010s.

She was one of the strongest advocates for a common European foreign and defense policy. “My passion is humanity,” she said in May 2025, when her hometown Bra granted her honorary citizenship. “I’ve got roots, I’ve got a homeland, a family, but precisely all that allows me to be a citizen of the world.”

She got involved with Arab women’s battle for equality in 2001 and started spending half her time in Cairo. She became fluent in Arabic — she had graduated in foreign languages at Milan’s Bocconi University — and built a network of intellectuals, politicians and prominent civil society figures.
She shared a humanitarian mission with Pope Francis

Never married, she maintained strong bonds with her family in Piedmont. “My father died before I could show him I could accomplish something,” she recalled in a 2020 interview with Vanity Fair. “He never understood my restlessness. He used to tell me: Emma, you are like Japanese poetry: beautiful, but I can’t understand it.”

In January 2015, she announced on Radio Radicale that she was suffering from lung cancer and was being treated with chemotherapy but didn’t plan to stop her political activity. In May of the same year, she said her cancer was in complete remission and eight years later appeared on a popular TV interview program announcing she was healed.
Over the years, Bonino cultivated a deep friendship with the late Pope Francis, despite their conflicting views on key ethical issues, including abortion and euthanasia.
In November 2024, Francis paid a home visit to Bonino — who had been just released from the hospital after treatment for respiratory problems — bringing her a bouquet of roses and chocolates.
A photo posted by Bonino on social media showed them both sitting in wheelchairs on her sun-drenched terrace in Rome.
Bonino said that during their conversations Francis always encouraged her to bring forward her humanitarian battles, defending those most in need.
When asked what battles she still needed to fight, Bonino used to say: “Many, too many. Human rights, world hunger, free scientific research ... Ten lives won’t be enough.”
Bonino is survived by her siblings, Domenica and Giovanni, and their children.

title: They led vigils to victims of Tiananmen. Now they’re facing time in prison for it.
summary: Three pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong who organized annual vigils for victims of China’s 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown were sentenced Friday under a national security law that critics say has stifled dissent.
